Best 4-Bay NAS in 2026 for Home and Office | Starry Hope Starry Hope 
 The Best 4-Bay NAS for Most Homes Is the UGREEN DXP4800 Plus
Updated on
 November 2, 2026,
by Jim Mendenhall 
 Bottom line 
 The UGREEN DXP4800 Plus is our pick for most homes. It has a 10GbE port, an Intel chip that transcodes video for Plex, and no drive restrictions. If the NAS will mostly back up your computers, the Synology DS925+ fits better, with software that needs little attention.
Recommendation
 At a similar list price, the DXP4800 GT suits a home with two fast computers to connect and little HDR video.
 A four-bay NAS gives you three times the usable space of a two-bay box with the same drives. With four identical drives in RAID 5, three drives’ worth of space holds data and the fourth drive’s worth holds parity, so the array survives one drive failure. Put the same drives in a two-bay box with RAID 1 and you get one drive’s worth of space.
 Close modal 
 Every price below is the list price for the box alone, diskless, as of early November 2026. Drives are extra, and four NAS-grade hard drives are a large part of the total cost, so price them before you pick a box.
 The five 4-bay NAS picks at a glance
 Model List price CPU Network M.2 slots Memory Video transcoding Software 
 UGREEN DXP4800 Plus $619.99 Intel Pentium Gold 8505 (2022) 10GbE + 2.5GbE 2x PCIe 4.0 8GB DDR5, max 64GB Intel Quick Sync UGOS Pro 
 UGREEN DXP4800 GT $659.99 AMD Ryzen Embedded R2514 (2022) 2x 10GbE 2x PCIe 3.0 x2 8GB DDR4, max 64GB, ECC capable Radeon Vega, HDR tone mapping in Plex untested UGOS Pro 
 Synology DS925+ $700.00 AMD Ryzen V1500B (2018) 2x 2.5GbE 2x, Synology SSDs only 4GB ECC DDR4, max 32GB None DSM 7.3 
 TerraMaster F4-425 Plus $649.99 (N150), $599.99 (N95) Intel N150 (2025) or N95 2x 5GbE 3x PCIe 3.0 x1 16GB DDR5 (N150), max 32GB Intel Quick Sync TOS 7 
 AOOSTAR WTR Pro 5825U $379.00 barebone AMD Ryzen 7 5825U (2022) 2x 2.5GbE 2x PCIe 3.0 x4 None included, max 64GB Radeon Vega, no HDR tone mapping in Plex None, bring your own 
 None of these chips is new. The newest is the Intel N150 from early 2025, and the Synology’s V1500B belongs to a family AMD launched in 2018. NAS makers use embedded and older laptop chips because they idle at low power and are cheap, and for file serving, photo backup, and a handful of containers, any of them is enough. The chip starts to matter when you want Plex to convert 4K video on the fly or want to run several virtual machines.
 UGREEN DXP4800 Plus pairs 10GbE with Quick Sync transcoding
 UGREEN NASync DXP4800 Plus
 Editor's Choice 
 4-Bay 10GbE 8GB RAM Intel Pentium Gold 8505 
 List price $619.99 | Full specs 
Check Price on Amazon
 The DXP4800 Plus lists at $619.99. Its Pentium Gold 8505 has one performance core and four efficiency cores, scores about 9,000 on PassMark’s CPU test, and includes Intel’s Quick Sync video engine. Plex’s own tone-mapping documentation lists Intel processors from Kaby Lake onward for hardware HDR-to-SDR conversion on Linux and NAS servers, so a 4K HDR movie can play on an older TV or a phone without washed-out colors. Plex needs a Plex Pass subscription for hardware transcoding; Jellyfin does it for free.
 One 10GbE port and one 2.5GbE port come on the board, so a desktop with a 10GbE card can copy files at around 1,100 MB/s once the drive array can keep up. The operating system lives on its own 128GB SSD, which leaves the four bays and two PCIe 4.0 M.2 slots free for data and gives TrueNAS or Unraid a separate drive to install on. Memory starts at 8GB of DDR5 and goes to 64GB across two slots, and there is no drive compatibility list: any SATA drive or NVMe SSD works.
 UGREEN’s software has less depth than Synology’s. Simon Handby at ITPro wrote that “UGOS Pro is extremely user-friendly, and generally quite capable, but it doesn’t have the depth you might expect from, say, Synology Disk Station Manager,” and counted 29 apps in its App Center. Plex installs through Docker rather than as a one-click package. Under a long, heavy load, KitGuru saw the CPU reach 100 degrees Celsius and the fan get loud, and measured about 24 watts at idle with four hard drives installed. The memory UGREEN labels “ODECC” is the on-die error correction built into every DDR5 chip, not ECC memory modules.
 UGREEN DXP4800 GT adds a second 10GbE port and ECC memory support
 UGREEN NASync DXP4800 GT
 Versatile 
 4-Bay 10GbE 8GB RAM AMD Ryzen Embedded R2514 
 List price $659.99 | Full specs 
Check Price on Amazon
 The DXP4800 GT launched in June 2026 and lists at $659.99, $40 more than the DXP4800 Plus. For that money it has two 10GbE ports, an AMD Ryzen Embedded R2514 that accepts ECC memory modules, and two bays that also take U.2 NVMe SSDs. Alastair Jennings at TechRadar edited video straight off it over 10GbE and called it “the best-value 4-bay NAS with 10GbE networking that I have seen yet.” PCWorld gave it an Editors’ Choice award and measured 25 watts at idle with the drives asleep and 40 to 42 watts in normal use.
 The Radeon Vega graphics transcode H.264 and H.265 for Plex, but Lon.TV’s tests of AMD’s Vega-based chips found that “hardware tone mapping is not supported on these chips,” so HDR movies look washed out when Plex converts them (Lon.TV did not test the R2514 itself). The 8GB memory module in the box is not ECC, so you have to buy ECC modules to get the protection, and a single module runs in single-channel mode. The OS sits on a 64GB eMMC chip soldered to the board, which makes a TrueNAS or Unraid install less straightforward than on the DXP4800 Plus. The two M.2 slots also run at PCIe 3.0 x2, about 2GB/s per SSD, against PCIe 4.0 on the DXP4800 Plus.
 Those limits matter less when your library is mostly SDR video or your TVs play HDR files directly, and in that case the GT’s second 10GbE port and ECC support are worth the extra $40 at list price. It is also the only box here that can link two machines at full 10GbE speed at once without a switch.
 Synology DS925+ has the strongest backup software
 Synology DiskStation DS925+
 Best for Backups 
 4-Bay 2.5GbE 4GB RAM AMD Ryzen Embedded V1500B 
 List price $700.00 | Full specs 
Check Price on Amazon
 The DS925+ runs DSM, Synology’s operating system. Its Hyper Backup app makes versioned, encrypted backups of the NAS to a USB drive, another NAS, or cloud storage. Active Backup for Business backs up Windows and Mac computers to the NAS, and Active Backup for Microsoft 365 does the same for Microsoft 365 accounts, both with no per-seat fee. Synology Photos, Synology Drive, and Snapshot Replication have years of fixes behind them. For a home or small office that wants a backup appliance and does not want to maintain Docker containers, none of the other four boxes ships with a comparable backup suite.
 Its chip is the oldest of the five, and its network ports tie the WTR Pro’s as the slowest. The Ryzen V1500B has no graphics engine, so Plex and Jellyfin transcode on its four CPU cores, which are too slow for 4K HEVC. The two 2.5GbE ports are the network ceiling for the life of the box, because it has no PCIe slot or network upgrade slot. Memory starts at 4GB of ECC DDR4 and tops out at 32GB. Dong Knows Tech found that “Its network throughput is generally limited by the 2.5Gbps ports,” and measured about 730 watt-hours per day with four hard drives, an average of about 30 watts.
 Drive support is better than at launch. Synology’s DSM 7.3 release in October 2025 restored storage-pool creation with third-party hard drives and 2.5-inch SATA SSDs, so WD Red and Seagate IronWolf drives work in the four bays. The two M.2 slots still take only Synology-listed NVMe SSDs for new pools and caches, per Synology’s drive compatibility policy . Synology’s cheaper four-bay, the DS425+ , uses a Celeron J4125 from 2019 with 2GB of memory; that is a step down from the DS925+ in both CPU and memory. Our UGREEN vs Synology comparison covers the software gap in more detail.
 TerraMaster F4-425 Plus has 5GbE and a cheaper N95 version
 TerraMaster F4-425 Plus
 Budget Pick 
 4-Bay 5GbE 8GB RAM Intel Processor N95 
 List price $599.99 | Full specs 
Check Price on Amazon
 The F4-425 Plus comes in two versions in the same aluminum case. The N150 model lists at $649.99 with 16GB of DDR5, and the N95 model lists at $599.99 with 8GB of DDR4. Both have two 5GbE ports, three M.2 NVMe slots, and Intel Quick Sync for Plex and Jellyfin, and both run TerraMaster’s TOS 7 or a third-party system such as Unraid. TOS includes TRAID, which mixes drive sizes in one array the way Synology’s SHR does.
 A 5GbE port carries about 500 to 550 MB/s, roughly double a 2.5GbE port, and it falls back to 2.5GbE or 1GbE on an older switch. The limits are the M.2 slots, which get one PCIe 3.0 lane each and top out just under 1,000 MB/s, the single memory slot, and the lack of a PCIe slot. Mark Pickavance at TechRadar wrote that “A few niggles, like the feet that fall off, suggest this product was rushed to market,” while Rob Andrews at NASCompares measured about 13 watts at idle with three SSDs and no hard drives.
 At list price the N150 model costs $30 more than the DXP4800 Plus, which has a faster CPU and a 10GbE port, so the N150 version is mostly a sale-price buy. The N95 model lists $20 below the DXP4800 Plus. The N95 model at $599.99 is the cheapest box here that ships with its own NAS software, though running more than a few containers on it calls for a memory upgrade.
 AOOSTAR WTR Pro 5825U has the fastest CPU and no software
 AOOSTAR WTR PRO 5825U
 Best Performance 
 4-Bay 2.5GbE No RAM AMD Ryzen 7 5825U 
 List price $379.00 | Full specs 
Check Price on Amazon
 The WTR Pro 5825U is a barebone four-bay box with an eight-core, 16-thread Ryzen 7 5825U, a laptop chip from 2022 with a PassMark score of about 17,774, double the DXP4800 Plus. It lists at $379.00 with no memory, no SSD, and no NAS software. Add two DDR4 SO-DIMMs and an NVMe drive for the operating system, then install TrueNAS, Unraid, Proxmox, or a Linux distribution yourself. In return you get enough CPU for several virtual machines and containers at once, two M.2 slots at PCIe 3.0 x4, and two 2.5GbE ports.
 The drive bays are not hot-swappable, so you have to power down to replace a failed drive, and Rob Andrews at NASCompares found the trays hard to use: “Trying to get a hard drive out of these trays is incredibly difficult.” Andrews measured 31 to 32 dBA at idle with four drives, and NotebookCheck measured 37 to 38 dB(A) at idle with no hard drives installed. There is no vendor app store, phone backup app, or remote-access service, and 10GbE means adding a USB adapter or giving up an M.2 slot to a network card.
 Close modal 
 Network speed limits file copies more than the CPU does
 A 2.5GbE port moves about 280 MB/s in practice. That is enough to stream any video file, back up phones, and serve a family’s documents, and it is about as fast as a single hard drive. Four hard drives in RAID 5 can read faster than that, so a 2.5GbE port becomes the bottleneck the moment you copy a large folder of photos or video from a desktop. A 10GbE port raises the ceiling to about 1,100 MB/s, and 5GbE sits in between.
 Faster ports only help if the rest of the path matches. A 10GbE NAS needs a 10GbE card or adapter in the computer and either a 10GbE switch or a direct cable between the two. If your router and switch are gigabit, every box here runs at about 110 MB/s until you upgrade them. Our article on 10GbE versus 2.5GbE for a home NAS works through when the upgrade pays off. The DS925+ has no way to add a faster port later, and the WTR Pro has no built-in route to 10GbE short of a USB adapter or an M.2 network card that gives up an SSD slot, while the two UGREEN boxes have 10GbE built in.
 RAID 5 or RAID 6 on four drives
 With four drives, RAID 5 gives you three drives of usable space and survives one failure. RAID 6 gives you two drives of usable space and survives two failures. The case for RAID 6 is the rebuild: when a drive fails, the NAS has to read every sector of the other three to rebuild the fourth, which can take a day or more on large drives, and a second failure during that window loses the array in RAID 5. NASCompares’ guide treats RAID 5 as reasonable for small arrays and leans toward RAID 6 as drives grow.
 For a typical home NAS with four drives of 8TB to 16TB, RAID 5 plus a separate backup is a reasonable choice, and RAID 6 is the safer one if you can give up the space. Either way, RAID is not a backup. It keeps the NAS running after a drive dies; it does nothing about a deleted folder, ransomware, a failed power supply, or a fire. Keep a second copy of anything you care about on a USB drive, another NAS, or cloud storage.

 Synology, QNAP, TerraMaster, ASUSTOR & UGREEN: Bare, Drive-Less Enclosures
 The enclosure and the drives are two separate purchases, and buying them separately is almost always the better value. You pick the exact capacity you want instead of paying a premium for a pre-populated bundle. This tracks current $/bay pricing on bare, drive-less enclosures across the five brands homelabbers and data hoarders actually buy, from 2-bay desktop units up through 8-bay rackmount chassis.  Sizing: How Many Bays Do You Actually Need
 Bay count is the number that matters most when comparing NAS enclosures across brands, which is why this page sorts by $/bay rather than raw price. It's the closest thing to an apples-to-apples unit of expansion headroom, since a cheap 2-bay unit and a pricier 8-bay unit can have wildly different value depending on what you need to store.
 2 bays covers basic mirrored redundancy (RAID1) with no room to grow. 4 bays is the sweet spot for most homelabbers, enough for single-parity redundancy (RAID5/SHR) with real usable capacity and a spare slot for expansion. 5-8 bays starts to matter once you're seriously data hoarding, where dual-parity redundancy (RAID6/SHR-2) protects against a second drive failing mid-rebuild, which becomes a real risk once you're running larger, older drives.

 Frequently Asked Questions
 Should I buy a bare NAS enclosure or one bundled with drives?
 Buying bare and sourcing your own drives, often from a dedicated drive tracker rather than the NAS vendor, is usually cheaper and lets you pick the exact capacity and drive model you want. A bundled unit can be a reasonable convenience if you'd rather not manually test and burn in drives yourself, but you'll typically pay a premium for that.
 How many drive bays do I actually need?
 2 bays gets you basic mirrored redundancy with no room to grow. 4 bays is the sweet spot for most homelabbers: enough for RAID5/SHR with real capacity and a spare slot. 5-8 bays starts to matter for serious data hoarding, where dual-parity redundancy (RAID6/SHR-2) protects against a second drive failing during a rebuild.
 Synology vs QNAP vs TerraMaster vs ASUSTOR vs UGREEN: What's the Real Difference?
 Synology has the most polished, locked-down software ecosystem (DSM) with broad app support, but costs more and has grown more restrictive about non-Synology-branded drives on newer models. QNAP offers more raw hardware per dollar and a deeper feature set, but has had more publicized security vulnerabilities, so timely firmware updates matter. TerraMaster and ASUSTOR are the budget-friendlier options with smaller software ecosystems, which appeals most to people planning to run their own OS instead of the stock firmware. UGREEN is the newest entrant, and it shows: aggressive hardware for the price (10GbE and even Thunderbolt 4 show up at lower price points than the competition), but its UGOS Pro software is younger and thinner than the other four, so it appeals most to buyers who plan to run TrueNAS or Unraid anyway.
 Can I run TrueNAS or Unraid on one of these instead of the stock OS?
 Many x86-based NAS enclosures (most QNAP, TerraMaster, ASUSTOR, and UGREEN units, and some Synology Plus-series models) can run TrueNAS SCALE or Unraid instead of, or alongside, the stock firmware. UGREEN's NASync line is a standard x86 machine under the hood and is explicitly marketed as friendly to this. Compatibility varies model to model though, especially for vendor-specific hardware like front-panel LED and LCD control. Search your exact model number plus "TrueNAS" or "Unraid" to see what other owners ran into.
 Should I worry about buying a used NAS enclosure?
 It's a relatively low-risk used purchase. The parts that actually wear out in a NAS (fans and the power supply) are common and usually inexpensive to replace, and the drive bay backplane rarely fails since it sees far less stress than the drives themselves. Just make sure all the drive trays are included: they're often proprietary to the model and hard to track down separately if any are missing. Also confirm the seller actually wiped the drives, since a used NAS' data destruction is on the previous owner, not you. If you're the one retiring an old NAS or its drives instead, see E-Waste Recycling for secure destruction and responsible disposal in Topeka and Shawnee County.
 What's the power draw like on a NAS enclosure?
 By the makers' own spec sheets, a 4-bay NAS draws about 35-42W with its drives active and 11-22W with them spun down, a 2-bay about 12-16W active, and 5- to 8-bay units about 43-54W. Running 24/7 at 40W costs about $65 a year at the U.S. average rate. My NAS power consumption table lists every model on this tracker, and the power cost calculator works out the cost at your own rate.

 Rules for Choosing a 4 -Bay NAS
 1 Start with 3 equal drives under SHR / RAID 5 to enjoy 1-drive parity while leaving 1 bay free for zero-downtime future expansion. 
 2 Use RAID 5 for media and backups to maximize capacity (75% usable). Choose RAID 6 / SHR-2 dual parity for irreplaceable business files. 
 3 If streaming 4K movies with subtitle transcoding, verify that the NAS processor features an Intel Quick Sync GPU. 
 4 Pair 4-bay systems with a compatible UPS (Uninterruptible Power Supply) to prevent array corruption during unexpected power outages. 
 Mistakes to Avoid Before Buying
 ✕ Filling all 4 bays on day 1 with small 2TB drives, eliminating easy expansion. 
 ✕ Choosing a non-iGPU processor (like AMD Ryzen V1500B) when intensive 4K Plex hardware transcoding is required. 
 ✕ Overlooking noise: 4 × 7200rpm drives can be audible in a bedroom; locate the NAS in an office or utility closet. 
 Frequently Asked Questions
 Why is a 4-bay NAS considered the best choice for home use?
 A 4-bay NAS hits the mathematical sweet spot: RAID 5 gives you 75% usable capacity (versus 50% in a 2-bay RAID 1 mirror), while providing full 1-disk failure protection. You can also populate 3 bays initially and preserve the 4th bay for hassle-free storage expansion.
 What is the cheapest 4-bay NAS in 2026?
 Enclosures like the TerraMaster F4-424 and UGREEN DXP4800 represent the most affordable modern 4-bay entry points with Intel processors, starting around $400 to $450 before hard drives.
 How much does a complete 4-bay NAS cost with hard drives?
 Use the exact-model cost table below the picks and compare both total spend and protected capacity. Three 12TB drives under single parity provide 24TB decimal capacity; four provide 36TB. Checkout prices, tax, shipping, backup storage, and network upgrades can change the final budget.
 Can I start a 4-bay NAS with just 2 hard drives?
 Some systems allow a two-drive mirror or SHR pool to grow by adding disks and migrating to single parity. The supported steps depend on the operating system and existing RAID layout; conversion is not automatic on every NAS. Read the model-specific procedure and verify your independent backup before changing the pool.
 What is the difference between RAID 5 and RAID 6 in a 4-bay NAS?
 RAID 5 allocates one drive worth of storage to parity (75% usable with 4 drives) and survives one disk failure. RAID 6 uses dual parity (50% usable with 4 drives) and survives two simultaneous drive crashes, which is recommended for mission-critical business retention or when rebuilding high-capacity 16TB+ arrays.

 The drives. Through 2026, Western Digital and Seagate pointed essentially all of their high-capacity (nearline) hard-drive output at AI and cloud, and consumer NAS drives took the hit. WD CEO Irving Tan told investors the company’s nearline capacity is “fully allocated through calendar year 2026,” with order books not reopening until the first half of 2027 ( winbuzzer.com, 2026-02-18 ; xda-developers.com ).  The RAM. DDR5 memory prices roughly tripled from late 2025 into 2026 as the same AI buildout consumed DRAM output.  A Synology DS425+ was $599.99 at Newegg on September 23, 2026 with zero storage, and a QNAP TS-464-8G $639.00 empty. Both lock you into proprietary software, both charge extra for features that should be free, and both come with a CPU you'd be embarrassed to put in a laptop. For less, the 5825U box with 16GB of RAM and a boot drive costs $526.78, with eight cores and your choice of operating system.
 On the Synology question specifically: the company's 2025 Plus and Value models (DS925+, DS1825+, DS425+) shipped with a drive-compatibility list that threw warnings on third-party Seagate and WD disks and pulled features. Synology reversed course in DSM 7.3 (October 2025) -- third-party drives work again on those 2025 models with full monitoring and alerts, and with every storage feature ( mjtsai.com, 2025-10-09 ). So the drives are not locked today. But Synology framed the reversal as "in the meantime" while it keeps testing additional drives, with no promise that 2026 models stay open. The read: the company walked it back under sales pressure, the lock-in instinct is still there, and building your own box sidesteps the whole question.
 The used enterprise hardware crowd will tell you to grab a retired Dell server. Fine, if you want 120W at idle and a machine that sounds like a hair dryer. The smart budget NAS in 2026 is a small 4-bay box with efficient silicon and an OS matched to your actual needs. Here's how to build one.
 The Hardware: Two Barebone Boxes That Make Sense
 The NAS enclosure market for DIY builders used to be terrible. You either bought a proprietary Synology/QNAP shell or hacked together a desktop case with drive cages. The AOOSTAR WTR Pro changed this. Two models, both with 4 SATA bays, dual 2.5GbE, and compact form factors designed specifically for NAS duty.
 Correction, September 24: The watts below are Notebookcheck's idle and load readings for each box. This page had printed them as readings at different drive counts and had called the Intel box an N100; Notebookcheck tested an N150.
 AOOSTAR WTR Pro N150 (was N100) — The Efficiency Pick, If You Can Find One
 Price: not listed on AOOSTAR's own store on September 23, 2026; $592.99 barebone from a Newegg marketplace seller
 CPU: Intel N150 (4C/4T, the N100's Alder Lake-N successor)
 RAM: 1× DDR5 SO-DIMM (add your own)
 Storage: 4× SATA bays + 1× M.2 NVMe
 Network: 2× 2.5GbE
 AOOSTAR has superseded the original N100 SKU with an N150 "upgraded N100" variant -- same Alder Lake-N efficiency class, a modest clock bump, the same ~6W-class TDP and Quick Sync iGPU. The Intel N100/N150 is the darling of the low-power homelab world and for good reason. This chip was designed for efficiency-first workloads. Notebookcheck tested an N150 unit (review published May 29, 2025) and measured 9.3W minimum, 14.3W average and 18.7W maximum at idle, and 24.6W average in 3DMark06 with a 27.9W peak in Cinebench R15 Multi. That's the whole system at the wall, CPU and board together.
 Four cores, four threads. No hyperthreading. For a NAS serving files over SMB and running a few Docker containers, that's plenty. Where it falls short is heavy transcoding or running a bunch of VMs alongside your storage — the N100 simply doesn't have the threads for it. If your NAS is a NAS and nothing more, the N100 is the right chip.
 The M.2 NVMe slot gives you a fast boot drive or ZFS SLOG/L2ARC cache. Dual 2.5GbE means you can bond two links or run one for management and one for data, which matters once your network is upgraded to 2.5GbE .
 Availability, September 23, 2026: AOOSTAR's store no longer lists the N150, so a new one comes from marketplace stock: $592.99 barebone from a Newegg marketplace seller. The 5825U at $379 direct is $213.99 cheaper and faster, which is why this guide leads with it.
 AOOSTAR WTR Pro 5825U — The Multitasker
 Price: $379.00 barebone direct from AOOSTAR on September 23, 2026 (regular $399.95); $512.99 plus $5.99 shipping from a Newegg marketplace seller
 CPU: AMD Ryzen 7 5825U (8C/16T)
 RAM: 2× DDR4 SO-DIMM, up to 64GB
 Storage: 4× SATA bays
 Network: 2× 2.5GbE
 At $379 direct it is the cheapest new 4-bay AOOSTAR, and the US-warehouse barebone was in stock on AOOSTAR's store on September 23. It comes with eight cores and sixteen threads. The Ryzen 7 5825U is a full mobile processor with real multi-threaded grunt. If you want your NAS to double as a lightweight homelab node (Plex transcoding, a few Docker containers, maybe a small VM), the 5825U gives you the headroom.
 The idle power story is more nuanced than the headline numbers suggest. Notebookcheck measured the 5825U WTR Pro at 5.5W minimum, 8.7W average and 13W maximum over a minute at idle, with a Metrahit Energy meter and a monitor attached. Its spec table lists the test unit's storage as one 512GB SSD and the review does not mention hard drives in the power test, so count your drives on top. Those idle numbers are lower than the N150's. minipc-review.com's review (August 22, 2026) prints higher plug readings for the 5825U: 15W to 18W at idle with only NVMe SSDs fitted, and 23W to 24W with four hard drives. It does not say who took them or with what meter.
 The catch is load power. Notebookcheck measured the 5825U at 46.2W average in 3DMark06 and a 67.5W peak (the peak came in a Prime95 stress run), against the N150's 24.6W 3DMark06 average and 27.9W Cinebench R15 Multi peak: about 1.9 times the N150's average and 2.4 times its peak. If you're doing heavy transcoding regularly, your electricity bill will notice. If your NAS mostly idles and occasionally serves files, the 5825U's lower idle draw in Notebookcheck's test means it's cheaper to run 24/7 than the N150.
 The 64GB DDR4 RAM ceiling is important for TrueNAS builds. ZFS loves RAM, and having two SO-DIMM slots means you can start with 16GB and upgrade to 64GB later by replacing it with two 32GB modules. The N100 model's single DIMM slot is more limiting.
 If you need more than four bays or 10GbE, AOOSTAR's newer WTR MAX (Ryzen 7 PRO 8845HS, 6+5 bays, dual 10GbE SFP+, USB4, Oculink) steps up to $659 direct from AOOSTAR (regular $699) on September 23, 2026, and $903.99 from a Newegg marketplace seller. It is past the budget brief here.

 Drives: Buy Two Now, Add Two Later
 A mirror (RAID 1 / ZFS mirror) gives you redundancy on day one and defers half the drive cost: $659.98 for the IronWolf pair now, and the other two bays stay empty until you need them. Which specific drives to buy (CMR vs SMR, the WD Red Plus vs IronWolf Pro tiers, and the recertified $/TB math) is its own decision, covered in depth in the best NAS hard drives guide .
 Seagate IronWolf 8TB (ST8000VN004): Amazon · Newegg , $329.99 at Newegg on September 23, 2026. CMR, 7200 RPM, includes IronWolf Health Management. A mirrored pair is $659.98 for 8TB usable. The faster 7200 RPM spindle runs a little louder.
 WD Red Plus 8TB (WD80EFPX): Amazon · Newegg , $345.00 at Newegg on September 23, 2026. Also CMR, 5640 RPM, designed for NAS duty. A mirrored pair is $690.00, $30.02 above the IronWolf pair.
 On September 23 the IronWolf was $15.01 a drive cheaper at Newegg, so buy the IronWolf unless the box sits in a room where you will hear a 7200 RPM spindle seek; then the WD is worth the $30.02. For a genuine budget build, recertified enterprise drives go further (see the next section). For drives of 20TB and up, where the rebuild time decides the layout, see the six-bay rebuild math .
 The 2026 Drive Question: New, Recertified, or Shuck?
 Because drives now dominate the budget, where you buy them is the most important call you'll make. Three routes:
 New NAS drives. IronWolf 8TB at $329.99 and WD Red Plus 8TB at $345.00, both at Newegg on September 23, 2026. Full manufacturer warranty, the quietest option, and zero homework. If your data is irreplaceable and you don't want to babysit drives, pay for new.
 Recertified enterprise (Seagate Exos and similar). This is the homelab budget path in 2026, and it's what the r/DataHoarder and r/truenas crowd actually buys during the shortage. Sellers like ServerPartDeals and goHardDrive move recertified enterprise disks at the best dollar-per-TB you'll find. If you're torn between a recertified Exos and a new IronWolf Pro, our NAS hard drive guide prices both in the same table. The caveats: warranties are shorter (often ~1-2 years, seller or limited manufacturer), enterprise 7200 RPM drives idle louder and warmer, and you should run a burn-in test the day they arrive. Redundancy matters more here -- run ZFS or parity and let the array absorb a bad drive. Plan capacity and parity with the NAS & RAID storage calculator , and if you're pairing this with Proxmox, the ZFS on Proxmox guide covers pool layout and scrubs.
 Shucking external drives. Pulling the bare drive out of a cheap external enclosure used to be the classic discount move. It still works, but the same shortage that lifted bare-drive prices has compressed the shucking discount, so the savings are thinner than they were in 2024. Worth a look on a deal; don't plan the budget around it.
 Picking Your NAS Operating System
 The hardware is the easy part. The OS decision is where most people get stuck, and the wrong choice can mean a rebuild six months in. All three are legitimate and built for different users; the four-way comparison with Proxmox goes deeper than this section, and the storage-backend guide covers running one inside the other.
 TrueNAS Community Edition — The ZFS Purist
 Price: Free (Community Edition)
 Minimum RAM: 8GB (for up to 8 drives; more is better)
 Filesystem: ZFS (mandatory — it's the entire point)
 ZFS gives you checksums and snapshots, scrubs the pool on a schedule, and is the most reliable storage layer available on consumer hardware. If data integrity is your primary concern — and for a NAS it probably should be — TrueNAS is the safest choice.
 The RAM requirement is real. ZFS uses ARC (Adaptive Replacement Cache) aggressively, and starving it below 8GB leads to poor performance. The old "1GB of RAM per TB of storage" rule overstates it for a home box: 16GB runs this build's 8TB mirror, and a full 4× 8TB array (32TB raw), with a few apps. The 5825U WTR Pro's 64GB ceiling and dual DIMM slots make it the better TrueNAS chassis.
 Community Edition is the Linux line that used to be called SCALE, and its apps run as Docker containers. Version 25.10.7 was the current download on September 23, 2026. The download page also documents the upgrade path from the FreeBSD-based CORE 13.0-U6.8.
 Unraid — The Flexibility Play
 Price: Starter $49 (6 devices) / Unleashed $109 (unlimited) / Lifetime $249
 Minimum RAM: 8GB (16GB+ recommended for VMs)
 Filesystem: XFS per drive, parity-based redundancy
 Unraid takes a fundamentally different approach to storage. Each drive is an independent XFS filesystem, and parity is calculated across drives. The practical advantage: you can mix drive sizes. A 4TB, an 8TB, and a 12TB can all live in the same array as long as the parity drive is the largest. Try that with ZFS or traditional RAID.
 The community app ecosystem is Unraid's real draw. Docker containers and VMs are first-class citizens with a point-and-click interface. Installing Plex, Nextcloud, or Home Assistant is a five-minute affair. For users who want a NAS that does everything and don't want to touch a terminal, Unraid is the most approachable option.
 The cost is real but reasonable. The Starter license at $49 covers 6 storage devices: the four bays and a cache SSD, with one to spare. For a 4-bay build, that's all you need. Unleashed at $109 removes the device limit; Lifetime at $249 also includes lifetime updates.
 The tradeoff versus ZFS: Unraid's parity system is slower for writes (parity calculated in real-time), and it doesn't offer ZFS-level checksumming or self-healing. For most home users serving media and backing up photos, this doesn't matter. For a business storing irreplaceable data, it might.
 OpenMediaVault — The Lean Option
 Price: Free
 Minimum RAM: 1GB (4GB comfortable / 8GB+ recommended)
 Filesystem: ext4, XFS, Btrfs, ZFS (via plugin)
 OMV is Debian with a web UI for NAS management. That's not a criticism — it's the lightest option by a wide margin. If you want a NAS and nothing else, OMV runs on almost nothing. The 1GB minimum is real: it will function on minimal hardware.
 For users who are comfortable in Linux and want a pure NAS without the overhead of TrueNAS or the cost of Unraid, OMV is the right call. It serves SMB and NFS shares, runs rsync jobs and handles basic Docker management. It doesn't try to be a hypervisor or an app platform.
 One important note: OMV is not supported in an LXC container . If you're planning to run it inside Proxmox , it needs a full VM. This matters for homelab users who want to consolidate a NAS into an existing Proxmox node.

 The Verdict
 On September 23, 2026 the 5825U TrueNAS build costs $1,186.76 with two IronWolf 8TB drives. A Synology DS425+ with the same two drives comes to $1,259.97, and a QNAP TS-464-8G to $1,298.98. The DIY box is $73.21 cheaper than the Synology and brings 16GB of RAM against the DS425+'s 2GB, and eight Ryzen cores against a quad-core Celeron.
 The gap is small, so buy the DIY box for its OS flexibility, the RAM and cores, dual 2.5GbE and room to repurpose the hardware. Recertified drives can cut the drive bill further, but the WTR Pro takes SATA drives only: skip SAS listings, and compare warranty as well as price.
 Both DIY builds are quieter than a Synology under load. Both give you the freedom to change your OS, upgrade components, and repurpose the hardware if your needs change.
 Build a NAS box that exactly fits the role
 If you’d rather pick parts yourself instead of buying a turnkey AOOSTAR, the TechFuelHQ PC Builder is a free, open-source picker with socket / RAM / PSU compatibility checks and a CC BY 4.0 parts dataset. Pair it with the Proxmox vs TrueNAS vs Unraid decision guide to pick the OS, and the 10GbE homelab networking guide if your storage is fast enough that 2.5GbE becomes the bottleneck. A DIY case with its own power supply needs sizing for spinning drives; the PSU wattage calculator counts each 3.5-inch drive at its 22W spin-up peak.
 Choose the NAS role before the chassis
 A cheap NAS is only a good value when its storage layout and software match the network and job. For a storage-first home server with two equal drives, start with the TrueNAS mirror build above. TrueNAS’s current hardware guide calls for at least 8GB of memory, a separate SSD boot device and two equal-size devices for one storage pool; this build clears those minimums.
 For an array that will grow one disk at a time or mix capacities, choose Unraid and make the parity disk at least as large as the biggest data disk, as the official array guide requires. For a small Debian-based file server where you are comfortable choosing the storage plugins yourself, use OpenMediaVault.
 Keep adjacent projects out of the base build until the role demands them. A rackmount chassis changes the noise and power plan along with the backplane and controller, so it is outside this compact four-bay brief. An SSD pool, 10GbE link or Plex transcoding box also needs its own workload decision. Use the NAS hard-drive guide for CMR and endurance choices, including warranty, the Plex and Jellyfin NAS guide for media hardware, and the 10GbE guide only after the storage side can outrun 2.5GbE.
 Once the parts are installed, follow the operating system’s own installer and storage-creation documentation rather than treating a buying guide as a setup wizard. Decide the pool or parity layout first, create shares second, then add apps. If Proxmox is part of the plan, use the storage-backend guide before installing either layer; virtualized storage changes which system should own the disks.
 Case, rack and all-flash NAS decisions
 For a DIY NAS case or bare server chassis, count usable drive bays after the motherboard, HBA, power supply and cables are installed. Check motherboard and PSU form factors, cooler height, HBA clearance, drive airflow, rail support and the rack’s usable depth. A hot-swap backplane also needs the right drive interface and enough controller links. TrueNAS’s hardware guide recommends direct disk connections where possible, at least 6Gbps SATA III for hot-swap backplanes, and an HBA or controller in passthrough/JBOD mode rather than hardware RAID.
 A rack NAS pays for density and front-accessible drives with more chassis depth and usually more fan noise. The compact four-bay 5825U build on this page is the fit for a living space or a shallow shelf. Choose rackmount only after measuring the rack and confirming rails, backplane, controller, PSU and acoustics from the exact chassis documentation. That checklist answers “server rack NAS” more reliably than calling one case universally best.
 For an SSD-based NAS, choose media and networking together. The TrueNAS guide notes that flash is much faster and insensitive to vibration, but says to size quality, power-loss safety and write endurance for the workload; NVMe devices can also need dedicated heatsinks. It warns against USB-connected SSDs as primary TrueNAS storage because device serials can be reported inaccurately. Native SATA, U.2 or M.2 bays with adequate cooling are the safer starting point. If the pool can outrun 2.5GbE, plan the 10GbE path at the same time.
 How to use the NAS from Windows, macOS or Linux
 Create the storage pool first, then make a dataset and a user account for the share. For Windows and mixed-device homes, SMB is the usual choice; NFS is the Unix-like option. TrueNAS warns against sharing the root or pool-level dataset, so create a child dataset and set its permissions before starting the SMB service.
 On Windows, enter \\nas-name\share-name in File Explorer or make it persistent with net use Z: \\nas-name\share-name /PERSISTENT:YES . On macOS, use Finder > Go > Connect to Server and enter smb://nas-name . On Linux, install the CIFS client package and mount //nas-name/share-name at a local mount point. TrueNAS documents all three paths in its SMB share guide . Give each person their own account and grant only the datasets they need.

 Frequently asked questions
 What is the best budget NAS for home use in 2026? For a turnkey 4-bay box, the AOOSTAR WTR Pro 5825U: $379 barebone direct from AOOSTAR on September 23, 2026, four 3.5-inch bays, dual 2.5GbE, 8.7W average idle in Notebookcheck’s test of an SSD-only unit, and it runs TrueNAS, Unraid or OpenMediaVault. The WTR Pro N150 costs more and does less: AOOSTAR’s own store no longer lists it, and a Newegg marketplace seller wanted $592.99 for the barebone that day. Drives are most of the bill. A Seagate IronWolf 8TB was $329.99 at Newegg and a WD Red Plus 8TB $345.00, so a mirrored pair runs $659.98 to $690.00 and four drives $1,319.96 to $1,380.00. The 5825U takes DDR4-3200 SO-DIMMs, $93.79 for 16GB at Newegg. The used alternative is a refurbished HP EliteDesk 800 G4 Mini ($272.22 on September 24, 2026, with an i5-8500T and 16GB, from a Newegg marketplace seller) with a USB-C drive enclosure, for replaceable media only.
 Do I really need ZFS for a home NAS? For two or more drives storing irreplaceable data — yes. ZFS detects bit rot, scrubs silently, and recovers from drive failure cleanly. Unraid’s parity array is simpler and supports mixed drive sizes but doesn’t checksum data. For one-drive media boxes, ext4 or btrfs is fine. The ‘must I run ZFS’ question really translates to ‘is the data on this NAS worth more than the day of setup time ZFS asks for.’
 TrueNAS vs Unraid vs OpenMediaVault for a budget NAS in 2026? TrueNAS Community Edition 25.10: free, ZFS-native, official Apps catalog, best for storage-first builds. Unraid 7.3: a one-time $49 to $249 licence, mixed-drive support, smoothest Docker UI — best when expansion path is uncertain. OpenMediaVault 8: free, Debian-based, lightest on RAM (runs on 2–4 GB) — best for small N100/N305 boxes and people comfortable with Linux. None of the three is wrong; they target different priorities.
 How much RAM does TrueNAS need? The classic ‘ZFS needs 1 GB per TB’ rule is misleading in 2026. 16 GB total handles a 4-bay 24–40 TB array running TrueNAS CE 25.10 with a few apps. 8 GB is the floor; below that the Apps catalog gets unstable. 32 GB only matters if you’re running dedup (don’t) or 10+ apps.
 Is 2.5GbE enough for a home NAS in 2026? For a spinning-disk array — yes. A single SATA HDD tops out around 200 MB/s and 2.5GbE delivers about 280 MB/s, so the cable is faster than the disks. The cutover to 10GbE is at the storage media (NVMe or SSD pool), not the workload. See the 10GbE homelab networking guide for when 10G pays off.
 Used Dell / HP / Lenovo mini PC plus USB DAS — is that a real NAS? Yes, with one caveat. On September 24, 2026 a refurbished HP EliteDesk 800 G4 Mini (i5-8500T, 16GB, 512GB SSD) was $272.22 at Newegg from SJ Computers LLC, and a Yottamaster 4-bay USB-C enclosure $157.61 delivered ($145.99 plus $11.62 shipping, unchanged since September 23), $429.83 together before drives. The caveat: USB attached storage is not as bulletproof as native SATA/HBA — occasional disconnects happen. For replaceable media, fine. For irreplaceable data, build the inside-the-box path instead. A used mini PC also sidesteps the 2026 RAM spike — you inherit its RAM instead of buying new.
 Why did a budget NAS get more expensive in 2026? Two shortages landed at once, and both trace back to AI data centers. First, Western Digital and Seagate redirected nearly all high-capacity hard-drive output to AI/cloud, and consumer NAS drives climbed 30–50% (WD’s CEO said nearline capacity is ‘fully allocated through calendar year 2026’). Second — the part most 2026 guides miss — DDR5 memory prices roughly tripled from late 2025 into 2026 as AI demand consumed DRAM supply: chip prices went from about $6.84/GB in September 2025 to about $27.20/GB by December, and analysts expect the crunch to last into 2027. On September 23, 2026 Newegg sold a 16GB DDR5-5600 SO-DIMM for $229.99 and a 16GB DDR4-3200 SO-DIMM for $93.79. The 5825U box held at $379. So in 2026 the budget fight is entirely about the two consumables — drives and RAM — not the box. Buy the box new; buy the drives recertified; buy exactly the RAM you need and no more.

TrueNAS or Unraid on a Mini PC (2026): Best DIY NAS Boxes | ComputingForGeeks

 Building a NAS yourself comes down to two decisions: what box to put it on, and whether to run TrueNAS or Unraid. Get those two right and a DIY NAS gives you more bays, more compute, and full hardware transcoding for a fraction of what a turnkey unit with the same specs costs. Get them wrong and you fight driver quirks, USB drop-outs, and a pool that rebuilds for a week. A UPS with graceful shutdown keeps a power cut off that list.
 Original content from computingforgeeks.com - post 169033 
 2026 makes the case stronger than it has been in years. A wave of small x86 NAS boxes (Aoostar, CWWK, Topton) now ship with Intel or Ryzen silicon, multiple SATA bays, 2.5GbE or 10GbE, and an open BIOS, so they run TrueNAS or Unraid out of the gate. At the same time Synology shipped its 2025 Intel models, the DS225+ and DS425+, without the Intel GPU driver in DSM, so they can no longer hardware-transcode Plex or Jellyfin on stock DSM, which is exactly the gap a DIY build fills. This guide ranks the hardware worth buying, settles the TrueNAS vs Unraid question, and walks through a TrueNAS install we ran end to end on 25.10 “Goldeye” in June 2026, with the Unraid 7.3 details checked in September 2026 and the hardware prices below checked again in October 2026.
 Short answer: yes, a mini PC makes a good NAS, as long as the drives sit on SATA or M.2 inside the box rather than on a USB enclosure. Run TrueNAS on a mini PC when your drives are matched and data integrity comes first; run Unraid on a mini PC when the drives are mixed sizes or you want to add one at a time. For a finished box, the Aoostar WTR Pro at about $400 is the easiest start, and the WTR Max at about $660 is the one to buy if you want ECC and 10GbE.
 Quick picks
 If you want the verdict before the reasoning, here it is. Every box below has an open BIOS and runs TrueNAS or Unraid; the drives and the OS are separate choices covered further down.
 Best overall, easiest to live with: Aoostar WTR Pro . A finished 4-bay box with hot-swap trays, dual 2.5GbE, and two NVMe slots. Around $400 for the barebones, check the live price.
 Best value, most bays per dollar: 6-bay i3-1115G4 NAS board . A CWWK-design ITX motherboard with six SATA ports, four 2.5GbE NICs, and a PCIe x4 slot for about $260. You supply the case and PSU.
 Best powerhouse, real ZFS machine: Aoostar WTR Max . Eight Ryzen cores, ECC support, dual 10GbE SFP+, and eleven drive positions. Around $660, check the live price.
 Best when you already own a mini PC: a TerraMaster D4-320 USB enclosure bolts four bays onto any machine for about $170. Read the USB caveat below before you point ZFS at it.
 The OS: run TrueNAS if data integrity is the priority and your drives are matched; run Unraid if you have mismatched drives or want to add one disk at a time. Both are excellent in 2026.
 How we built and tested this
 The hardware picks were checked against each manufacturer’s spec sheet and a live retailer listing, and every Amazon link here was confirmed against the exact model before it went in. Prices move weekly during the 2026 storage and memory shortage, so each one is a band with a link to the live listing rather than a number that ages badly.
 The software half is hands-on. We installed TrueNAS 25.10 “Goldeye” (build 25.10.4; install whatever 25.10 point release is current) on a fresh machine, carved four disks into a RAIDZ1 pool, created datasets, shared one over SMB, and opened the app catalog. The screenshots later in this guide are from that build, not from marketing pages. Unraid 7.3 was used for the comparison facts and licensing; both projects shipped a current stable release within the last few weeks.
 TrueNAS vs Unraid: which OS to run
 This is the decision that shapes everything else, because it dictates how your drives are organized and how you grow later. Both are mature and both run Docker apps and VMs. They differ on filesystem and flexibility. Our TrueNAS vs Unraid comparison tests both on the same box, including mixed drive sizes, adding one disk later and what each does about bit rot.
 TrueNAS (the free Community Edition, formerly called SCALE) is built on ZFS. You get end-to-end checksums, scheduled scrubs that catch silent corruption, snapshots, and replication. The cost of that safety is rigidity: a RAIDZ group treats every disk as the size of the smallest, so you want matched drives, and although you can now expand a RAIDZ group one disk at a time, the older data keeps its original parity ratio until you rewrite it.
 Unraid takes the opposite stance. Its array is a set of independent disks protected by one or two parity drives, so you can mix a 8TB, a 12TB, and a 20TB drive in the same array and add another whenever you like, as long as no data disk is larger than your parity disk. That flexibility is why it owns the “I bought drives over five years and none of them match” crowd. The trade-off is that the default XFS array has no block checksums (you can opt into btrfs or ZFS per disk), and Unraid is paid software.
 Factor TrueNAS (Community Edition) Unraid 7.3 
 Cost Free, open source $49 / $109 / $249 one time, optional $36/yr updates 
 Device limit None Starter: 6 storage devices; Unleashed and Lifetime: unlimited 
 Boot device Dedicated SSD (USB sticks discouraged) USB flash, or internal NVMe/SSD since 7.3 
 USB-attached data disks Avoid for primary storage Allowed in the array, same USB reliability caveat 
 Filesystem ZFS only XFS (default), btrfs, or ZFS per disk 
 Mixed drive sizes Penalized (vdev = smallest disk) Yes, freely 
 Add one disk at a time Yes (RAIDZ expansion, with a parity-ratio caveat) Yes, native 
 Data integrity Strongest (checksums, scrub, snapshots) Parity rebuild, optional btrfs/ZFS checksums 
 RAM 8 GB minimum, ECC recommended Lighter, no ZFS RAM demand unless you choose ZFS 
 Plex/Jellyfin transcoding Yes, pass the iGPU into the container Yes, pass the iGPU into the container 
 Best for Maximum safety, matched disks, snapshots Mixed disks, easy growth, media servers 
 For most people the split is simple. If you are buying a matched set of drives and you care most about your data surviving a bad disk or bit rot, run TrueNAS. If your drives are a mixed bag or you plan to add capacity a disk at a time, Unraid earns its license fee. Mind the tier on small builds: the $49 Starter license covers six storage devices, so a six-bay board plus an NVMe cache pool already needs the $109 Unleashed tier. On the TrueNAS side, version 26 was still in beta in September 2026, so a new pool belongs on the 25.10 stable release. One note worth pulling out: a frequent point of confusion is ECC RAM on TrueNAS. TrueNAS strongly recommends it, but the docs are explicit that it is not required, and plenty of home pools run fine without it.
 1. Aoostar WTR Pro: best overall
 The WTR Pro is the box we point most people at because it removes the part beginners dread: there is no case to source, no PSU to match, no drive cage to wire. It arrives as a finished 4-bay enclosure with hot-swap trays, and you add RAM, an NVMe boot drive, and your disks.
 Aoostar WTR Pro: a finished 4-bay box with hot-swap trays, dual 2.5GbE, and two NVMe slots. Image: Aoostar. 
 The pick to buy is the AMD Ryzen 7 5825U barebones model. Eight cores handle a stack of containers and a Plex library without breaking a sweat, the two M.2 NVMe slots let you mirror a boot drive or run a fast cache pool, and the four SATA bays take drives up to 24TB each. Two DDR4 SO-DIMM slots take up to 64GB. Hardware transcoding runs through the Radeon iGPU over VA-API, which Jellyfin handles natively; Plex needs Plex Pass for any hardware transcoding, and its AMD support on Linux is unofficial, so an Intel QuickSync box is the safer Plex pick.
 Who it is for: anyone who wants a NAS that looks and behaves like an appliance but runs the OS they choose. Skip it if: you want more than four spinning disks, or you specifically need Intel QuickSync, in which case the Intel N150 version of the WTR Pro is the cheaper, lower-power, QuickSync-equipped alternative, mainly sold direct by Aoostar. Note that the N150 version has a single RAM slot, while the 5825U model linked here has two.
 2. 6-bay i3-1115G4 NAS board: best value
 If you are comfortable putting parts in a case, nothing touches the price per bay of a NAS motherboard. This one is a CWWK design (the board silkscreen reads CW-TGL-NAS) sold on Amazon under the UDPTCP brand: a mini-ITX board with the CPU soldered on, six SATA ports, two NVMe slots, four 2.5GbE NICs, a PCIe 3.0 x4 slot, and two DDR4 SO-DIMM slots for up to 64GB of non-ECC memory, and it sells for around the price of an empty 4-bay turnkey chassis.
 6-bay i3-1115G4 NAS board: six SATA ports, four 2.5GbE NICs, two NVMe slots, PCIe x4. Image: manufacturer listing. 
 Read the CPU line before you buy, because it moved. The 8-core i3-N305 version of this board is no longer stocked on Amazon; what is in stock is the Tiger Lake build around a Core i3-1115G4, two cores and four threads with Intel UHD graphics. QuickSync transcoding is still on the table and file serving barely notices, but two cores is not the headroom the N305 gave you for a busy app stack, so size your container load accordingly. About $260 for six bays is still the standout number here. Four of those SATA ports come off a JMB585 controller through an SFF-8643 breakout cable rather than board-edge connectors, which is included but worth knowing before you plan cable routing. The listing had no customer reviews yet in late September, so buy it where returns are easy. CWWK also sells its boards directly, including higher-core variants, if the Amazon listing does not have the chip you want.
 If six SATA ports is not enough, the board’s PCIe x4 slot takes a SAS HBA, and one card adds eight more drives; our HBA card guide for TrueNAS covers which cards run in IT mode and which cables they need. The case sets the ceiling on bays either way, and the NAS case roundup sorts the options from four-bay ITX cubes to twelve-bay towers.
 Who it is for: the builder who wants the most drives per dollar and already has a small case and an SFX power supply, or is happy to buy them. Skip it if: you want a plug-and-play box. Two honest gotchas to plan for: add-on SATA controllers such as the JMB585 often hold the CPU out of its deepest package sleep states, so idle power can sit a few watts higher than the chip alone would suggest, and six spinning drives draw a surge at power-on, so pick an ATX or SFX supply (the board takes standard 24-pin plus 4-pin power) with headroom on its SATA rail.
 The one part the board does not include is a home for the drives. The Jonsbo N3 is the case most builders pair it with: a mini-ITX NAS cube with eight 3.5-inch bays (two more than the board’s six ports, so you have headroom), two built-in fans, and room for an SFX power supply. It runs around $160, check the live price.
 Jonsbo N3: a mini-ITX NAS case with eight 3.5-inch bays, the usual home for the CWWK board. Image: Jonsbo. 
 Add the case, a stick of RAM, and a small boot SSD and you have a six-bay NAS for less than a finished four-bay appliance costs.
 3. Aoostar WTR Max: best powerhouse
 The WTR Max is what you buy when the NAS is also going to be your virtualization host and you want to run ZFS the way it is meant to be run. It is built around the Ryzen 7 PRO 8845HS, eight cores and sixteen threads, and crucially it supports ECC memory up to 128GB across two DDR5 slots.
 Aoostar WTR Max rear I/O: dual 10GbE SFP+, USB4, and OCuLink alongside six SATA and five M.2 bays. Image: Aoostar. 
 The connectivity is the headline. Two 10GbE SFP+ ports plus two 2.5GbE, USB4, and an OCuLink port for external PCIe, with six SATA bays and five NVMe slots for eleven drive positions in total. ECC plus 10GbE plus that many bays is territory Synology and UGREEN simply do not sell at this price, which lands around $660 for the barebones (check the live price). The Amazon listing linked here is Aoostar’s own store with only a few units left in mid-October, so if it sells out, Aoostar sells the same barebones direct at the same price. Transcoding runs on the Radeon 780M through VA-API, which Jellyfin handles well; Plex on AMD under Linux is unofficial, so plan on Jellyfin if transcoding matters on this box.
 Who it is for: the ZFS builder who wants ECC, 10GbE, and room to grow into a real homelab. Skip it if: you only need file storage; the extra cores, ECC, and 10GbE are wasted money if nothing will use them. For the layout choices that make the most of this many bays, our ZFS RAID levels guide covers how mirrors and RAIDZ trade capacity against rebuild safety.
 4. A mini PC plus a TerraMaster D4-320: if you already own a mini PC
 If there is already an Intel mini PC on your desk doing light duty, the cheapest way into a NAS is to hang drives off it. The TerraMaster D4-320 is a 4-bay USB 3.2 Gen2 enclosure that connects over a single 10Gbps Type-C cable, and at around $170 it turns any machine into a four-disk NAS.
 TerraMaster D4-320: four bays over a single 10Gbps USB-C cable, pure JBOD passthrough. Image: TerraMaster. 
 There is a caveat that has to be stated plainly: USB-attached disks are not a good home for ZFS. USB-to-SATA bridges can drop or renumber devices and hide drive serials and SMART data, which is exactly the information ZFS relies on to handle errors, and a dropped device mid-write can fault a pool. The D4-320 is actually the safer style of enclosure for this because it does pure JBOD passthrough with no RAID firmware in the way, but treat it as a budget or Unraid-array path for non-critical data, not as the foundation for an important TrueNAS pool. Our DAS and JBOD enclosure guide sorts enclosures by how each bay is bridged, which decides whether ZFS sees real serials and SMART data.
 Who it is for: the person with a capable mini PC already running and a tolerance for the USB caveat. If you want a deeper look at the small machines that pair well here, our homelab mini PC roundup covers the boxes worth basing this on. Skip it if: this is your primary copy of anything you cannot lose.
 5. UGREEN NASync DXP4800 Plus: buy turnkey, run DIY
 There is a middle path between building from parts and accepting a locked-down appliance: buy a turnkey x86 box that ships with an open BIOS, then wipe its OS and install TrueNAS or Unraid. The UGREEN NASync DXP4800 Plus is the box that made this popular. It is a finished four-bay unit with a built-in 10GbE port alongside 2.5GbE, two NVMe slots, a 128GB internal SSD, and an Intel iGPU that keeps QuickSync. Its BIOS is open, which is why the DXP4800 Plus became a favorite box to flash TrueNAS or Unraid onto. UGREEN’s position on whether a third-party OS affects the hardware warranty has been inconsistent, so confirm that with UGREEN before you wipe the stock system.
 UGREEN NASync DXP4800 Plus: a turnkey 4-bay box with built-in 10GbE and an open BIOS that flashes to TrueNAS or Unraid. Image: UGREEN. 
 Who it is for: the reader who wants appliance fit and finish, built-in 10GbE, and Intel transcoding, but not Synology’s software lock-in or a parts list. It sells for around $660, check the live price. Skip it if: you want the most bays per dollar, which the CWWK board still wins. And if you would rather keep a polished vendor OS and not flash anything at all, the best NAS for home and self-hosting roundup weighs the DXP4800 Plus against Synology and the rest as turnkey units.
 The rest of the parts: drives, boot SSD, and RAM
 The box is half the build. Three more decisions finish it.
 Drives are where the money goes and where mistakes hurt. Buy CMR NAS drives and avoid drive-managed SMR, which can stall a RAID or ZFS rebuild for days; our CMR vs SMR breakdown explains why, and the best NAS hard drives guide lists the safe models by capacity. HDD prices climbed 30 to 50 percent through 2026, so buy the capacity you need now rather than waiting for a dip that is not coming this year.
 A small NVMe drive handles the OS and apps. TrueNAS wants a dedicated boot device (modern versions write to it enough that USB sticks are discouraged), and a WD Blue SN5100 500GB , two generations on from the SN580 (the SN5000 came in between) and built on QLC flash rather than the SN580’s TLC, is plenty for boot plus an app or cache pool. Check who is selling it before you buy: small NVMe listings on Amazon have been showing marketplace prices far above normal, and any 256GB to 500GB NVMe drive does the job. Unraid is the exception: it traditionally boots from a USB flash drive with the license tied to that stick, and since 7.3 it can also boot from an internal NVMe, SSD, or eMMC device with a TPM-based license, which frees the USB port and removes the flash drive as a failure point.
 RAM sizing follows the OS. TrueNAS wants 8GB as a floor and is happier with 16 to 32GB once apps are running; Unraid is content with less. A 32GB DDR4 SO-DIMM (two for 64GB) covers the DDR4 boxes here. Crucial’s single 32GB DDR4-3200 stick had no live Amazon listing in mid-October, so the link goes to its 64GB kit of two 32GB DDR4-3200 SO-DIMMs , sold through a third-party seller. Fair warning: the 2026 memory shortage has that kit at about $500 in mid-October, roughly $250 a stick and far above 2025 prices, so budget the RAM and boot SSD as seriously as the box itself.
 How to turn a mini PC into a NAS
 If you already own a mini PC, the conversion is mostly a question of where the drives connect. Internal SATA or M.2 is the path that works with either OS. A USB enclosure is the fallback when the box has no room, and it limits what you should trust to it: TrueNAS’s own hardware guide says to avoid USB-connected disks for primary storage, partly because USB bridges can report drive serial numbers inaccurately.
 Count the internal slots. Most mini PCs have one or two M.2 slots and at most one 2.5-inch SATA bay. Two NVMe drives in a mirror make a small, fast, fully supported NAS; spinning disks need a NAS-style box or an enclosure.
 Pick the boot device. TrueNAS takes a whole drive for boot, so a two-slot machine gives one M.2 to boot and one to data unless you add storage. Unraid 7.3 can boot from USB or an internal drive.
 Add bulk storage. For disks, a JBOD USB 3.2 enclosure like the D4-320 is the budget route. Use it for an Unraid array or backup copies, and keep irreplaceable data on internal SATA or NVMe.
 Install the OS and build the pool. Flash the installer to a USB stick, install to the boot drive, then create the pool or array from the web UI. The TrueNAS walkthrough below shows each screen.
 Protect it. Put it on a UPS that the OS can read over USB, and set up a backup that leaves the box.
 Install TrueNAS and create your first pool
 Once the parts are together, TrueNAS is the faster of the two to get running, so it is the one we walk through. The installer is a short text menu: pick the boot SSD as the destination, set a password for the truenas_admin account, choose legacy or EFI boot to match your firmware, and reboot. Mini PCs often ship with Secure Boot on, so disable it (or set it to Other OS) in the BIOS first, or the installer will not boot. The console then prints the web address to open in a browser.
 The dashboard is the landing page. It confirms the version, the CPU and memory, and the health of everything at a glance.
 The first real task is the storage pool. Under Storage, the Create Pool wizard lists the disks it can use; we selected the four data drives and chose RAIDZ1, which keeps the array alive through a single disk failure. The result is a healthy pool named tank , reported here as one RAIDZ1 group, four wide.
 A pool on its own is just space. You carve it into datasets, which are the unit you snapshot, share, and set quotas on. We created a media dataset and a backups dataset under the pool.
 To reach a dataset from other machines, you share it. An SMB share is the right default for a mixed network of Windows, macOS, and Linux clients. We shared the media dataset and started the SMB service, which the Shares page shows running. TrueNAS will not serve SMB to root or its built-in accounts, so first create a user under Credentials > Users with SMB Access enabled; that account is the one clients log in with.
 From a Linux client, install the CIFS tools ( cifs-utils from apt or dnf), create a mount point, and mount the share as that SMB user to confirm it works:
 NAS_IP = 192.168.1.50 
SMB_USER = nasuser 
sudo mkdir -p /mnt/media 
sudo mount -t cifs // ${ NAS_IP } /media /mnt/media -o username= ${ SMB_USER } 
 The last piece that makes a DIY NAS worth more than an appliance is the app catalog. TrueNAS moved to Docker-based apps, and the Discover page lists around 385 of them, Plex and Jellyfin and Immich and Nextcloud among them, each a few clicks to deploy onto your pool.
 That is the whole loop: install, pool, dataset, share, apps. Everything after that, the snapshots, the replication jobs, the containers, builds on those same five screens.
 What to get right before you buy
 A few decisions matter more than the brand on the box.
 Match bays to a five-year plan, not today. A 4-bay box feels roomy until a media library outgrows it, and adding bays later means a new chassis. If you can see yourself wanting more than four drives, start with six or buy the WTR Max.
 CMR drives, never drive-managed SMR. This is the one non-negotiable. SMR drives can take days to rebuild into an array and sometimes drop out mid-rebuild, turning one failed disk into a data-loss event. Stay inside the NAS-branded lines and you are safe.
 Decide on ECC honestly. ECC adds a layer of protection against memory errors corrupting data on the way to disk. TrueNAS recommends it but does not require it, and only the WTR Max on this list takes it, and only with true ECC SO-DIMMs rather than standard memory. For irreplaceable data it is worth the box that takes it; for a media server it is a nice-to-have.
 Confirm transcoding if you run Plex or Jellyfin. Hardware transcoding turns a 4K stream from an 80 percent CPU pin into a 10 percent one. Every Intel box here has QuickSync; the Ryzen boxes transcode through VA-API, which Jellyfin supports well and Plex supports only unofficially on Linux. Plex hardware transcoding also needs Plex Pass. Either way, you have to pass the GPU device into the container, which both TrueNAS and Unraid support.
 Right-size RAM and the network. 2.5GbE is the floor in 2026 and saturates a couple of spinning drives; 10GbE only pays off with NVMe or a wide array and a switch to match. Give TrueNAS 16GB or more once you add apps.
 Protect it and connect it. A ZFS pool hates an abrupt power cut, so put the NAS on a pure sine wave UPS such as the CyberPower CP1500PFCLCD , which TrueNAS reads over USB and uses to shut the pool down cleanly when the battery runs low. To actually use those 2.5GbE or 10GbE ports you also need a switch that speaks the same speed, like the TP-Link TL-SG108S-M2 , a fanless eight-port 2.5G unmanaged switch in a metal case. Check the live price on both.
 Plan for noise and power. The spinning drives, not the CPU, set both the idle wattage and the sound. A four-drive box idles quietly, but pack six or eight disks and the spin-up surge and the steady hum become real, so a case with decent fans and staggered spin-up earns its place.
 Remember that RAID is not a backup. A RAIDZ pool survives a dead disk. It does not survive ransomware, a fat-fingered delete, or a house fire. Keep to the 3-2-1 rule: three copies, on two kinds of media, one of them off-site. ZFS snapshots and replication cover the on-box layer nicely, but something still has to leave the building.
 Pairs with Best Synology Alternatives: UGREEN vs QNAP vs UniFi UNAS vs DIY

 Which one should you build?
 Strip away the detail and three clear paths remain. If you want the least friction, buy the Aoostar WTR Pro , drop in matched CMR drives, and run TrueNAS; it behaves like an appliance and protects your data properly. If you are counting every dollar and do not mind assembly, the CWWK 6-bay board gives you six bays for the price of an empty enclosure. If the NAS is also your homelab, the Aoostar WTR Max with ECC and 10GbE is the one you will not outgrow.
 On software, let your drives decide: matched disks and a low tolerance for data loss point to TrueNAS, a pile of mismatched drives points to Unraid. And if a finished, supported box still sounds better than building one, the best NAS for home and self-hosting roundup covers the turnkey options worth buying instead.

 by Joule P. Kraft · July 30, 2026 · updated October 22, 2026 
 As an Amazon Associate, and through other affiliate programs (including SONOFF), I earn from qualifying purchases. No affiliate relationship influences my recommendations.

 I have run a NAS in my house for the better part of a decade, and in that time the box in the closet has quietly become the most important piece of hardware I own. It holds every photo my family has taken, every document I would cry to lose, the Plex library that keeps the TV happy, and a growing pile of self-hosted apps that replaced a dozen cloud subscriptions. So when someone asks me which NAS to buy on a budget in 2026, I do not treat it as a small question. This is the machine your digital life sits on, and the market shifted hard this year in a way that changes the old easy answer.
 The short version is this. The reflexive advice for years was just buy a Synology, and for Plex in particular that advice is now wrong. Synology gutted hardware transcoding on its newest models and tightened its drive compatibility, so the brand that used to be the safe default is the one I now steer media-focused buyers away from. In its place, UGREEN and TerraMaster came in with Intel chips, real Quick Sync transcoding, faster networking, and open enough software that you can run their OS or wipe it for TrueNAS. These are the five budget NAS options I would actually put my own money on today, and just as importantly, which one fits which kind of person.
 What actually matters in a budget NAS in 2026
 Before the picks, let me tell you what I look at, because spec sheets are noisy and most of the numbers do not matter. Three things decide whether a budget NAS is good, and everything else is detail.
 The first is the CPU, specifically whether it has Intel Quick Sync. If you plan to run Plex or Jellyfin and stream to phones, tablets, or an older TV, your NAS will need to transcode, which means re-encoding video on the fly into a format the client can play. Quick Sync is Intel’s hardware engine that does this cheaply and quietly, and a small Intel chip with Quick Sync will out-transcode a much beefier CPU that lacks it. This single feature is why the recommendations moved this year. An ARM-based NAS or a crippled-GPU Synology will choke on the exact job most people buy a NAS to do.
 The second is drives and bays. A NAS is storage first, and how many drives it holds decides how much you can store and how safe that storage is. Two bays gives you a mirror, which survives one dead disk. Four bays gives you room to grow and better redundancy math. I nudge most people to four bays even if they start with two drives, because expanding later is painful and drives are the cheapest part of the whole equation over the life of the box.
 The third is the software and how locked down it is. A prebuilt NAS lives or dies on its operating system and app store. Synology’s DSM is still the nicest software in the category, which is the whole reason people put up with the hardware regressions. UGREEN and TerraMaster ship younger software that is improving fast, and crucially they let you wipe it and install TrueNAS or Unraid if you would rather own the stack. That escape hatch matters, because it means the hardware is never wasted even if you outgrow the vendor’s OS.
 UGREEN NASync DXP4800 Plus: the best all-around pick
 This is the one I hand people who ask for a single answer. The UGREEN NASync DXP4800 Plus is a four-bay NAS built around an Intel Pentium Gold with Quick Sync, so it handles real 4K HDR transcodes that Synology’s current lineup cannot touch. It takes up to 64GB of DDR5, has two M.2 NVMe slots for a fast cache or all-flash pool, and it is the only NAS on this list with built-in 10GbE alongside a 2.5GbE port. That combination of transcoding muscle, memory headroom, and networking is genuinely rare at this price.
 What sells me is the flexibility. UGREEN’s own NASync software has matured into a clean, Synology-style experience with an app store, photo sync, and backup tools, so you can treat it as a turnkey appliance out of the box. But because it exposes standard hardware, you can also wipe it and run TrueNAS Scale or even Unraid, turning it into a proper virtualization and storage host. You are not locked in, which is exactly what I want from a box I plan to keep for five years. Check current price before buying: it is not the cheapest thing here, but it is the one I would least likely regret, and it is the machine that pairs perfectly with a compute-focused mini PC Proxmox node .
 UGREEN NASync DXP2800: the best cheap Plex box
 The UGREEN NASync DXP2800 is the value play, and it is the model I see recommended over and over in the self-hosting communities right now. Check its current price before deciding what to spend on your first server. It is a two-bay unit on an Intel N100, which is the same efficient little chip powering half the good budget mini PCs on the market, and critically it includes Quick Sync. That means a NAS that transcodes Plex properly, sips power, and stays quiet enough to live on a shelf in a living room.
 You give up bays and expansion compared to the DXP4800 Plus. Two drives means a mirror and not much room to grow, and there is a single M.2 slot rather than two. But for a household that wants a Plex server, phone photo backups, and a handful of self-hosted apps, this is plenty, and the N100 has enough headroom to run a few Docker containers without complaint. This is the NAS I recommend to friends who are nervous about the hobby and do not want to overspend before they know they will stick with it. It does the core job well and leaves the door open to upgrade later.
 TerraMaster F4-424 Pro: the best base for TrueNAS or Proxmox
 If you already know you want to run TrueNAS, Unraid, or Proxmox and treat the vendor OS as disposable, the TerraMaster F4-424 Pro is the smart buy. It packs an Intel Core i3 N305, an eight-core chip that is a real step up from the N100 in both raw compute and transcoding headroom, into a four-bay chassis with dual M.2 slots and support for 32GB of DDR5. On paper it undercuts the UGREEN four-bay while giving you nearly as much hardware.
 The reason I frame it as a TrueNAS base rather than a general recommendation is TerraMaster’s own software, TOS, which is functional but the weakest of the prebuilt operating systems here. The good news is that the F4-424 Pro exposes a standard UEFI BIOS, so you can plug in a USB stick and install TrueNAS Scale or Proxmox VE cleanly, and that is exactly how most enthusiasts run it. Do that and you get a powerful, open four-bay box that will happily host a ZFS pool, a stack of containers, and a couple of VMs; check current price before buying. If you want a turnkey appliance experience, buy UGREEN. If you want a strong x86 foundation to build your own stack on, this is the value leader.
 Synology DS224+: still fine, but know what you are buying
 I cannot write this list without addressing Synology directly, because it is still what most people type into a search box first. The Synology DS224+ is a competent two-bay NAS with an Intel Celeron J4125 that does include Quick Sync, and its DSM software remains the best in the business for backups, Time Machine targets, and the excellent Synology Photos app. If your priority is a rock-solid, low-fuss backup and file-sync appliance for the family, it earns its place and I still recommend it in that role.
 But be clear-eyed about why it is on this list and where it sits. This is an older-generation model, and the reason I point media buyers at UGREEN instead is the direction Synology has taken its newer units, stripping usable transcoding and locking down drive compatibility. The DS224+ still transcodes because it predates that shift, but it is a two-bay box with limited memory and a CPU that will feel its age on heavy 4K libraries. Buy it for what DSM does beautifully, which is quietly protecting your data. Do not buy it expecting it to be the transcoding monster the UGREEN and TerraMaster boxes are, and do not assume the newer Synology models are a safe upgrade, because for Plex they are a step backward.
 The DIY TrueNAS build: the best value per terabyte
 For the person who cares most about maximum storage for the least money and enjoys the tinkering, nothing prebuilt beats rolling your own. A DIY TrueNAS build can start with an Intel N100 mini PC or a small ITX board, a few sticks of RAM, and either a drive cage or a cheap HBA card to add SATA ports. Put TrueNAS Scale on it and you get ZFS, the same enterprise-grade filesystem the expensive units run, with snapshots, checksums, and self-healing, and you get it with zero license fees and zero app lock-in.
 The honest trade is time and support. You are the one choosing parts, flashing an HBA, and reading forum threads when a pool will not import. There is more upfront friction than plugging in a UGREEN and clicking through a wizard. But the payoff is real. Dollar for dollar and terabyte for terabyte, a DIY box wins, especially once you get to six or eight drives where prebuilt units get expensive fast. This is also the build I point people to when they want ECC memory for maximum data integrity, since most prebuilt budget units do not offer it. If you already have a spare mini PC lying around, the marginal cost to turn it into a capable NAS is small, and it is a fantastic way to learn how storage actually works before you spend real money.
 How to pick between them
 Cut through all of it with a few questions. If you want one box that does everything well and you do not want to think hard, buy the UGREEN DXP4800 Plus. If you want the cheapest thing that still transcodes Plex properly, buy the UGREEN DXP2800. If you are set on TrueNAS or Proxmox and want the strongest x86 base for the money, buy the TerraMaster F4-424 Pro. If your job is backups and file sync for the family and you love polished software, the Synology DS224+ is still a fine appliance. And if you want the most storage per dollar and enjoy the build, roll a DIY TrueNAS box.
 Whatever you choose, remember two things I learned the expensive way. First, a NAS with no backup is not a backup, so plan for a second copy of anything irreplaceable, whether that is a cloud sync or an external drive you rotate. Second, protect the box from power problems with a proper UPS for your NAS , because a hard shutdown mid-write is one of the few things that can genuinely corrupt a storage pool. The NAS is the foundation, and it is worth building on carefully.
 The Bottom Line
 The story of NAS buying in 2026 is that the safe default changed. For years the answer was Synology, and this year that answer broke for anyone who cares about Plex, because Synology stripped the transcoding and tightened the drive locks that made its boxes worth the premium. UGREEN and TerraMaster stepped straight into that gap with Intel chips, real Quick Sync, faster networking, and software open enough to run their OS or your own. If I had to spend my own money today on one budget NAS to anchor a self-hosting setup, it would be the UGREEN NASync DXP4800 Plus, with the DXP2800 as the value pick and a DIY TrueNAS box for anyone who wants to build. Buy the one that matches how you actually work, put a backup and a UPS behind it, and it will quietly run your digital life for years.
 Where to Buy
