Prices and availability are subject to change.
 Frequently Asked Questions
 What is the best budget NAS for Plex in 2026? + For most people it is the UGREEN NASync DXP2800 if you want cheap and simple, or the DXP4800 Plus if you want room to grow. Both use Intel chips with Quick Sync, which is what actually matters for Plex, because Quick Sync is the hardware transcoding engine that lets one small box turn a 4K file into a stream your phone or old TV can play without melting the CPU. The important 2026 twist is that Synology quietly crippled transcoding on its newest models, so the old default answer of just buy a Synology no longer holds if media is your main job. If you only care about backups and file sync, a Synology DS224+ is still fine, but for Plex I steer people to UGREEN or TerraMaster now.
 Why should I avoid the newest Synology models for Plex? + Because Synology removed or disabled the hardware transcoding that made them the classic Plex pick. The 2025 and 2026 generation either ships with no usable GPU or has Quick Sync switched off in software, so a file that needs transcoding leans entirely on a weak CPU and stutters. Synology also started restricting which drives you can use in newer units, which pushes you toward their branded disks at a markup. Their DSM software is still excellent for backups, Time Machine, and photo sync, so I do not tell people to throw out a Synology they own. I just stop recommending the current lineup for anyone whose top priority is transcoding media.
 Should I buy a prebuilt NAS or build my own with TrueNAS? + Buy prebuilt if you want it working the same evening and you value support, a clean app store, and a small quiet box. Build your own if you want the most storage per dollar, full control of ZFS, and no software lock-in, and you are comfortable spending an afternoon in a BIOS and a config screen. A DIY TrueNAS box on an Intel N100 mini PC plus a drive cage often beats a prebuilt on raw value, especially at higher drive counts. The catch is that you are your own support desk. For a first NAS where you are still learning, I usually suggest a prebuilt UGREEN or TerraMaster, then build a DIY box later once you know what you actually use.
 How many drive bays do I need for a home NAS? + Two bays is the honest floor and it covers a lot of homes, giving you one drive of redundancy in a mirror so a single disk failure does not lose data. But two bays fills up fast once you add a Plex library, phone backups, and a few VMs, and expanding a two bay unit usually means replacing both disks. Four bays is the sweet spot I point most self-hosters to, because it lets you start with two drives and grow, and it supports better redundancy layouts. Go past four only if you are hoarding large media libraries or running many services. Remember that a NAS is for storage, and compute heavy work is often better on a separate mini PC.
 Do I need 10GbE networking on my NAS? + Most people do not, at least not yet. A single spinning hard drive tops out well under what 2.5GbE already delivers, so 2.5GbE is the right default for a 2026 home NAS and it is now cheap and common. You start to want 10GbE when you run an all flash NAS, edit large video files straight off the box, or move huge datasets between machines regularly. The nice thing about a unit like the UGREEN DXP4800 Plus is that it includes 10GbE, so you can start on 2.5GbE and light up the faster port later when the rest of your network catches up. Match the NAS to your switch, not to a spec sheet you will not use for two years.

 Frequently Asked Questions
 Is RAID a backup? ▼ No — this is the most important thing to understand about NAS. RAID (except RAID 0) protects against a single drive dying, keeping the array online while you replace the disk. It does nothing against accidental deletion, ransomware, corruption, theft, fire, or a power surge — all of which hit the live array and every mirror at once. RAID is for uptime; a backup is a separate copy you can restore from. Follow the 3-2-1 rule: 3 copies, 2 media types, 1 off-site.
 How many bays do I need — 2 or 4? ▼ A 2-bay NAS in RAID 1 (mirror) gives you one drive's worth of usable space with single-drive redundancy — plenty for photos, documents, and backups for most homes. Choose a 4-bay if you want more total capacity, two-drive redundancy (RAID 6 / SHR-2), or room to expand by adding drives later. Remember RAID redundancy is not extra capacity you get for free — a 2-bay mirror 'costs' half its raw space to redundancy.
 Does 2.5GbE actually matter, or is 1GbE fine? ▼ It matters more than most specs. A 1GbE port tops out around 110–118MB/s, but a single modern hard drive already reads at ~180–280MB/s — so on gigabit you're throttling the drive by half, and an array or NVMe cache even more. 2.5GbE roughly matches one fast HDD (~280MB/s) and makes large transfers dramatically quicker. For home NAS it's the most worthwhile speed upgrade; 10GbE only pays off with NVMe pools or big arrays.
 What's the deal with Synology and third-party drives? ▼ With its 2025 models (DS225+, DS425+, DS925+) Synology introduced a verified-drive policy that at launch restricted drives not on its list. DSM 7.3 relaxed it: per Synology's policy FAQ, hard drives and 2.5-inch SATA SSDs that are not on the list can now be used for new storage pools on the 2025 DiskStation Plus models, but M.2 NVMe SSDs must be on the list to create a pool or cache, and Synology only guarantees full functionality with listed drives. QNAP, TerraMaster, Asustor, UGREEN and DIY boxes have no such list. Check the exact model's current policy first.
 Do I need ECC RAM in a home NAS? ▼ No, it's a nice-to-have, not a requirement. ECC corrects single-bit memory errors and is reassuring on always-on systems with lots of RAM and irreplaceable data. But the 'ZFS needs ECC or it destroys your data' claim is a myth — ZFS is safer with ECC yet doesn't require it, and non-ECC boxes protect data for millions of users. A tested backup protects your data far more than ECC does. Treat ECC (as on Synology's DS925+) as a bonus, not a must-have.
 What's CMR vs SMR, and why should I care about drives? ▼ Every NAS ships empty — the drives are a separate, important purchase. Use NAS-rated CMR (conventional) drives like WD Red Plus or Seagate IronWolf. Avoid SMR (shingled) drives in a RAID array: SMR rewrites whole zones on write, which can make a RAID rebuild crawl or fail — dangerous, since a second drive can die during the rebuild. The plain WD Red (non-Plus) and many cheap desktop/shucked drives are SMR, so confirm CMR on the spec sheet.
 Should I buy a turnkey NAS or build a DIY TrueNAS box? ▼ Buy turnkey (Synology, QNAP, etc.) if you want an appliance: polished software, mobile apps, easy setup, low power, and vendor support, accepting weaker hardware-per-dollar and some lock-in. Go DIY with TrueNAS on a mini PC or built box if the homelab is the hobby or you need real horsepower: far more CPU/RAM per dollar, ZFS on your terms, and no drive lock-in — at the cost of doing your own setup, updates, and troubleshooting. Several boxes here (TerraMaster, UGREEN) explicitly support running TrueNAS.
 Can a NAS run Docker containers and VMs for self-hosting? ▼ Most x86 (Intel/AMD) boxes here can. The Celeron/N-series and low-power AMD chips comfortably run a handful of lightweight Docker containers (Pi-hole, media apps, small databases) with 4–8GB RAM; full virtual machines or many heavy containers want a stronger CPU and 8–16GB+. ARM-based budget NAS units and some entry models can't run VMs or full container platforms. If self-hosting is the goal, pick an x86 NAS with expandable RAM.

 The Best Budget NAS in 2026, Priced With Two Drives
Updated on

by Jim Mendenhall 
 Bottom line 
 The UGREEN DXP2800 is our budget NAS pick for most homes that want Plex, photo backup, and a few apps. It costs a little more than the cheapest two-bay boxes, and it adds two SSD slots and a faster network port. A household that only needs backups can save money with the cheaper UGREEN DH2300.
Recommendation
 Pair the DXP2800 with two 8TB NAS drives if the budget allows, since two 4TB drives cost less but fill up sooner.
 The UGREEN DXP2800 is our pick for most homes on a budget, and with two NAS hard drives the whole setup costs about $770 to $1,110. Two drives are the smallest setup that survives a drive failure, so every total below includes them. Hard drive prices roughly doubled over the past two years, and a pair of 4TB NAS drives now costs about as much as the DXP2800 itself. That shrinks what the cheaper boxes save. The DXP2800 adds $120 to $150 to the total over the cheapest two-bay setup, and the money buys a faster network port, an Intel chip that transcodes video, and two SSD slots.
 Every price below is a maker’s list or store price for the box, plus a rounded range for the drives as of October 2026. Drive prices move by tens of dollars from week to week.
 What the cheapest NAS setups cost with two drives
 The table pairs each box with two 4TB NAS drives (about $380 to $480 for the pair) and two 8TB NAS drives (about $660 to $720). In RAID 1, the mirror layout for two drives, two 4TB drives give you 4TB of usable space and two 8TB drives give you 8TB, because every file is written to both drives.

The DXP2800 setup costs about $120 to $150 more and gives the same 4TB with a 2.5GbE port, a chip that runs Plex and Docker, and two M.2 SSD slots. With 8TB drives the gap between those two setups stays the same in dollars and shrinks as a share of the total.
 The two four-bay boxes in the table cost $210 to $270 more than the DXP2800 and do not need all four drives on day one. Two drives in a four-bay box leave two empty bays for later, which matters more now that the cheapest way to add space is to add a drive rather than replace both.
 Our budget pick is the UGREEN DXP2800

 The UGREEN DXP2800 costs $389.99 on UGREEN’s store, marked down from $439.99, and runs on an Intel N100, a four-core chip from 2023 with Intel Quick Sync, the video engine that lets Plex or Jellyfin convert a 4K movie for a phone or an older TV without loading the CPU. It ships with 8GB of DDR5 in one slot (16GB maximum), a 2.5GbE port, two M.2 NVMe slots, and tool-less 3.5-inch trays in a metal case. A 2.5GbE port moves about 280 MB/s, close to the 300 MB/s that TechRadar gives as the practical ceiling for two hard drives striped together. A 1GbE port tops out near 115 MB/s.
 UGREEN’s UGOS Pro software includes a Docker app, so Immich, Home Assistant, or Pi-hole can run next to the file shares. The M.2 slots take an SSD cache or a separate SSD pool for those apps. UGREEN also lets you install TrueNAS or Unraid without voiding the warranty, so you can switch systems later without buying new hardware. OCinside measured about 7 W at idle in its December 2024 review , so the box itself costs about $10 a year to run at 17 cents per kWh; two spinning drives add more, and our 24/7 power cost math covers how to price that at your local rate.
 Two bays mean RAID 1 or RAID 0 only, so growing past two drives means replacing both with larger ones. There is no PCIe slot, so the only route past 2.5GbE is a USB network adapter. UGOS Pro has fewer apps than Synology’s DSM, and Plex and Jellyfin install as Docker containers rather than one-click packages. How-To Geek’s review of a pre-release unit in April 2024 said UGOS “needs a lot of work”; Docker and most of the missing features arrived in later updates, and Macworld’s July 2025 review called the interface intuitive but found UGOS Pro less mature than Synology’s and QNAP’s systems.
 The UGREEN DH2300 is the cheapest box and suits backups only
 The UGREEN DH2300 launched in 2025 at $209.99, and in October 2026 UGREEN’s store lists it at $269.99, on sale for $239.99. It runs UGOS Pro on a Rockchip RK3576, an eight-core ARM chip, with 4GB of RAM soldered to the board and a single 1GbE port. TechRadar’s November 2025 review by Mark Pickavance gave it 4.5 out of 5 and called it “a terrific NAS that does most of what these things are bought for, without breaking the bank.”
 It handles phone photo backup, a shared folder, and nightly PC backups. TechRadar measured 118 MB/s over the built-in 1GbE port with two 4TB IronWolf drives. With a USB 2.5GbE adapter (about $25), reads rose to 296 MB/s and writes to 286 MB/s. TechRadar also found that a cheap SATA SSD can act as a read cache for a single hard drive.
 The RAM cannot be upgraded, and UGREEN’s product page says the DH2300 does not have official Docker support or virtual machines. TechRadar wrote that with 4GB “it can only handle a couple of major Docker containers.” The ARM chip cannot run Windows or Linux virtual machines, and there are no M.2 slots. Even with a $25 USB 2.5GbE adapter, the DH2300 setup costs about $95 to $125 less than a DXP2800 setup, about 11% to 16% of the DXP2800 setup’s total with 4TB drives.
 The TerraMaster F2-425 is the cheapest Intel two-bay
 The TerraMaster F2-425 sits between the two UGREEN boxes. It pairs an Intel Celeron N5095 from 2021 with 4GB of DDR4 (16GB maximum), a 2.5GbE port, and TerraMaster’s TOS software, and TerraMaster’s store lists it at $299.99 with sales to about $255. Because it is an Intel chip, it runs Docker and virtual machines and has Quick Sync for video transcoding. PCWorld’s October 2025 review by Jon L. Jacobi called it “a good value for streaming media over your home network, handling IP cams, and backing up your computer,” and listed “occasional interface rough spots” and an “all-plastic case” as its cons.
 It has no M.2 slots, and its chip is two years older than the N100 in the DXP2800. At sale prices it is about $135 below the DXP2800. That buys Plex and a couple of containers if you can do without SSD slots. At its $299.99 list price the gap to the DXP2800 shrinks to $90, and the DXP2800 is the better use of that money.
 Four-bay boxes leave room for two more drives

Check Price on Amazon

 List price $659.99 | Full specs 
Check Price on Amazon
 A two-bay NAS has one upgrade path: replace both drives with larger ones and copy the data across. A four-bay box lets you start with two drives in RAID 1 and add two more later, or move to RAID 5, where one drive’s worth of space protects the rest. If your photo and video library keeps growing, adding drives to empty bays avoids retiring a working pair of drives. Our NAS comparison chart treats four bays as the practical starting point for a home NAS, and that holds for anyone who can see past 8TB. On a tight budget, a two-bay box is the cheaper entry.
 Close modal 
 The TerraMaster F4-425 Plus in its Intel N95 version lists at $599.99 with 8GB of DDR4, three M.2 NVMe slots, and two 5GbE ports, which is faster networking than any other box in this guide except the DXP4800 GT. The N95 is a 2023 chip in the same class as the DXP2800’s N100, with Quick Sync. The cons are a single RAM slot, M.2 slots that each run at one PCIe lane, and no PCIe slot for a 10GbE card.
 The UGREEN DXP4800 GT lists at $659.99 and moves to an AMD Ryzen Embedded R2514 with two 10GbE ports and ECC memory support. It is the only box here with 10GbE, which only pays off if your PC and switch also have 10GbE. It transcodes H.264 and H.265 video, but PCWorld’s review measured about 25 W with the drives asleep, so it costs more to run around the clock than the Intel N-series boxes.
 For tinkerers there is also the AOOSTAR WTR PRO 5825U , a four-bay barebone at $379 with an eight-core Ryzen 7 5825U and dual 2.5GbE. It ships with no RAM, no SSD, and no NAS software, so the full cost is $379 plus a DDR4 kit and a boot SSD, plus an evening installing TrueNAS or Unraid. The bays are not hot-swappable, so you power it down to change a drive. It is a poor fit for anyone who wants a setup wizard.
 Drive prices doubled, and small drives cost the most per terabyte
 Close modal 
 The NASDisks price tracker reports that the typical NAS hard drive of 8TB and up went from $21 per terabyte in July 2024 to $47 per terabyte in October 2026, more than double. MakeUseOf’s September 2026 report traces the cause to data center demand: “Western Digital says it’s sold out of nearline hard drive capacity through calendar 2026.” Analysts cited in that report do not expect prices to normalize before late 2027, so waiting for a sale is a weak plan.
 At the cheaper end of each size, a 4TB NAS drive costs roughly $48 to $60 per terabyte, an 8TB drive about $41 to $45, and 12TB drives fall to about $36. The 4TB pair is still the lowest total outlay. If you can spend about $250 more, the 8TB pair doubles your usable space for about 60% more on the drives.
 The drives to look for are CMR models sold for NAS use, such as WD Red Plus, Seagate IronWolf, or Toshiba N300. CMR (conventional magnetic recording) drives handle the long rebuild a RAID mirror runs after a drive swap. Plain WD Red drives (without “Plus”) in the 2TB to 6TB range use SMR (shingled magnetic recording), which writes slowly under sustained load and can stretch a rebuild into days. Recertified enterprise drives were the budget trick of 2024 and 2025, and they no longer help much. PC Server and Parts tracked a recertified 24TB Seagate Exos going from $298.99 to $699 in a year.
 SSD prices rose too. NASCompares’ July 2026 roundup shows 4TB NVMe SSDs that sold for about $190 to $230 in June 2025 listed at about $699 to $900 or more. At those prices, an all-SSD NAS costs far more per terabyte than one with hard drives.
 Where Synology and a mini PC fit
 Synology’s cheapest two-bay, the DS223j, runs Synology’s DSM software on a Realtek RTD1619B with 1GB of RAM and a 1GbE port. When TechRadar reviewed the DH2300 at its $209.99 launch price, it noted the DS223j cost “a few dollars less” and had a weaker chip and a quarter of the memory. Its draw is DSM’s backup apps, such as Hyper Backup and Snapshot Replication. Synology’s two-bay DS225+ starts near $400, the same price as a DXP2800, with a 2019 Celeron and 2GB of RAM; see our UGREEN vs Synology comparison for that matchup.
 A used office mini PC with TrueNAS or Unraid is cheaper still for the box: off-lease Dell OptiPlex and Lenovo ThinkCentre Micro models sell for $100 to $200. They hold one or two internal drives, have 1GbE, and need a USB enclosure for more disks, which is a weaker setup for a RAID mirror than a NAS with dedicated drive bays. Our guide to using a mini PC as a NAS covers that route, including the Beelink ME Mini , a small box with six M.2 SSD slots. The ME Mini was a cheap NAS in 2025, but with 4TB SSDs now costing several times a 4TB hard drive, it has become a pricey way to buy capacity.
 Which budget setup to buy
 For most homes, the setup we would choose is the UGREEN DXP2800 with two 8TB NAS drives, at roughly $1,050 to $1,110. If that is too much, two 4TB drives bring the total down to roughly $770 to $870 and still give you a working mirror. Nothing cheaper in this guide pairs Quick Sync video transcoding and Docker with SSD slots and a 2.5GbE port.
 Someone who only wants a home for backups and shared files can spend less. The UGREEN DH2300 with two 4TB drives comes to about $620 to $750, and a $25 USB 2.5GbE adapter is worth adding if your PC has a 2.5GbE port. If your files could outgrow 8TB within a few years, the TerraMaster F4-425 Plus N95 model with two drives makes more sense, because adding two drives later costs less than replacing both drives in a two-bay box.
 Whatever you buy, a RAID 1 mirror protects you from a dead drive, not from a deleted folder, ransomware, or a house fire. Keep a second copy of the files you cannot replace on a USB drive or a cloud backup service.  Best overall: TerraMaster F4-424 Pro
 The F4-424 Pro is the pick when transcoding is the job. Per TerraMaster’s spec sheet, its Core i3-N305 pairs a 32-execution-unit Intel UHD iGPU with 8 GB of DDR5 that expands to 32 GB — more headroom than the Celeron-class boxes it undercuts on price. In practice that translates to roughly four to five simultaneous 4K-to-1080p transcodes, and about half that if Plex is tone-mapping HDR to SDR at the same time.
 Who it suits: households with a mix of clients — an Apple TV 4K, a couple of phones, a browser tab — where somebody is always forcing a conversion. Main trade-off: TerraMaster’s TOS software is less polished than Synology’s DSM or QNAP’s QTS, and the third-party app catalog is thinner. You are buying silicon, not software.
 Best value four-bay: QNAP TS-464
 The TS-464 uses a Celeron N5095 with a 16-EU iGPU, 8 GB of DDR4 (16 GB max), dual 2.5GbE ports and two M.2 NVMe slots for cache or a separate metadata volume. It handles two to three 4K transcodes comfortably and will direct-play everything you throw at it. QTS is a mature platform with a proper container station, which matters if you want to run Plex alongside the *arr stack.
 Who it suits: the buyer who wants a proven four-bay chassis and doesn’t want to learn a new operating system. Main trade-off: roughly half the transcoding throughput of the N305 for only about $50–$100 less, and QNAP’s firmware cadence means occasional update babysitting.
 Best small starter box: Synology DS224+
 The DS224+ is the cheapest route into genuine Quick Sync transcoding. Its Celeron J4125 and 12-EU iGPU will push one, occasionally two, 4K-to-1080p conversions, and DSM remains the easiest NAS operating system to live with. The catch is the 2 GB of soldered RAM — plan on adding a stick to reach the 6 GB ceiling, because Plex’s metadata and thumbnail database is memory-hungry.
 Who it suits: a first NAS for one or two viewers, or a secondary box for a bedroom. Main trade-off: two bays means RAID 1 gives you only one drive’s worth of usable capacity, and there is no upgrade path except replacing the whole unit.
 Best for large 4K libraries: UGREEN NASync DXP4800 Plus
 The DXP4800 Plus is the only pick here with 10GbE built in, and its Pentium Gold 8505 carries a 48-EU iGPU — the strongest transcode engine in this group, good for five to six simultaneous 4K-to-1080p conversions. DDR5 expands to 64 GB, which is overkill for Plex but welcome if you also run virtual machines. The 10GbE port matters more than it sounds: a 4K remux peaks around 80–100 Mbps, so a 1GbE link saturates at roughly nine direct streams before overhead, while 10GbE removes the network as a bottleneck entirely.
 Who it suits: anyone with a 20 TB-plus remux collection and a wired 10GbE switch or a direct-attach workstation. Main trade-off: UGOS is the youngest operating system in this roundup, and the ecosystem is still catching up on polish.
 Best for direct-play purists: Synology DS923+
 Per Synology’s spec sheet, the DS923+’s AMD Ryzen R1600 has no integrated graphics — which means no Quick Sync, which means every conversion falls to two cores of CPU. Software-transcoding 4K HEVC on that chip is not realistic; it will stutter. But if your clients all direct-play, the DS923+ is arguably the best pure file server here: ECC memory support, a PCIe slot for a 10GbE card, and DSM’s mature storage management.
 Who it suits: a library encoded in formats your players already understand, or a household that keeps a separate mini-PC as the Plex server and uses the NAS purely for storage. Main trade-off: buy it expecting to transcode and you will be disappointed.
 How to choose: the numbers that actually matter
 1. Confirm you need transcoding at all
 Direct play uses no CPU — the NAS just streams bytes. Transcoding happens when the client can’t handle the file’s codec, container, resolution or subtitle format, or when remote viewers are capped by upload bandwidth. Check your library and your players first; if everything direct-plays, you can spend the transcoding budget on drive bays instead.
 2. Budget for Plex Pass, because hardware transcoding is locked behind it
 Plex’s documentation is explicit: GPU-accelerated transcoding is a Plex Pass feature. Without it, the iGPU sits idle and Plex falls back to software encoding. A lifetime pass costs roughly the same as one extra drive, and it is the single highest-value purchase in this entire build.
 3. Count bays by capacity, not by ambition
 A 4-bay chassis in RAID 5 or Synology’s SHR gives you three drives of usable space plus one for parity. A 2-bay in RAID 1 gives you one. If your library is 15 TB and growing, two bays means buying two 20 TB drives to store 20 TB — four bays means four 8 TB drives to store 24 TB, usually for less money.
 4. Match the network port to your peak bitrate
 Add up the peak bitrate of your busiest simultaneous streams and leave 30% headroom. Three 4K remuxes at 90 Mbps is 270 Mbps, which 1GbE handles fine. Ten of them is 900 Mbps, which it does not — that is when 2.5GbE or 10GbE stops being a luxury.
 Worked example: sizing a 4-bay NAS for a 400-film 4K library
 Assume 400 UHD remuxes at an average of 60 GB each. That is 24,000 GB, or about 24 TB of media. Add Plex metadata: artwork and database files run a few gigabytes, but generated video thumbnails can consume 100 GB or more on a large library, so budget 25 TB total.
 Four 12 TB NAS drives in RAID 5 give 36 TB raw usable, minus roughly 10% for filesystem overhead, landing near 32 TB. That leaves about 7 TB of growth room. At typical 2026 pricing of $15–$20 per terabyte for NAS-rated CMR drives, the storage costs $720–$960, on top of a $450–$650 chassis — call it $1,200–$1,600 all in, or roughly $3–$4 per film stored.
 Now the transcoding side: a 16-EU Celeron iGPU handles two to three 4K-to-1080p conversions; a 32-EU i3-N305 handles four to five; a 48-EU Pentium Gold handles five to six. Enable HDR tone mapping and cut every one of those numbers roughly in half, because tone mapping is a second GPU pass on the same silicon.

 Ownership realities: what wears out and what trips people up
 Drives fail first. NAS-rated CMR disks are typically rated around one million hours MTBF, which in a four-drive array usually means one failure somewhere in years three to five. Buy drives from different batches and keep a cold spare on the shelf.
 Avoid SMR drives. Shingled magnetic recording drives stall badly during RAID rebuilds. Check the spec sheet for “CMR” before you buy — this is the most common costly mistake in budget NAS builds.
 SSD cache is not a transcoding upgrade. It accelerates metadata and random I/O, not GPU work. If you have two M.2 slots, one cache drive plus one dedicated volume for Plex metadata is a better split than two mirrored cache drives.
 RAID is not a backup. It survives a dead disk; it does not survive an accidental delete, ransomware, or a power surge. Follow 3-2-1: three copies, two media types, one off-site.
 Heat and dust are the slow killers. Keep ambient temperature under 30°C, clean the intake filters every three to six months, and expect fans to be the first non-drive component to need replacing.
 Wire it. Wi-Fi adds jitter and typically halves usable throughput; a NAS on wireless will stutter on high-bitrate 4K even when the CPU is idle.
 Frequently Asked Questions
 Can I run Plex on a NAS without an Intel CPU?
 Yes, but only with software transcoding. AMD-based units like the Synology DS923+ handle direct play perfectly well and can serve several 4K streams at once, since streaming without conversion costs almost no CPU. The moment a client forces a 4K HEVC conversion, however, a low-power AMD chip will not keep up and playback will buffer.
 Do I really need a Plex Pass for hardware transcoding?
 Yes. Plex’s documentation lists GPU-accelerated transcoding as a Plex Pass feature, so without a subscription the integrated GPU stays idle and everything falls back to CPU encoding. This is why two NAS units with identical processors can perform completely differently — the difference is the license, not the hardware.
 How many simultaneous 4K streams can a NAS handle?
 Direct play is limited by disk and network, not CPU: on 1GbE expect roughly five to nine concurrent 4K remux streams before the link saturates. Hardware transcoding is limited by the iGPU: two to three streams on a 16-EU Celeron, four to five on a 32-EU Core i3-N305, and five to six on a 48-EU Pentium Gold. Enabling HDR tone mapping roughly halves each figure.
 Is RAID enough to protect my media library?
 No. RAID protects against a single drive failure by keeping the array running; it does nothing about deletion, corruption, theft or fire, because every change is mirrored instantly to the parity drive. Treat RAID as uptime insurance and keep a separate backup — for a large remux library, an external drive rotation or a second NAS at another address is the practical approach.
 How much RAM does a Plex NAS actually need?
 Plex itself is light, but the metadata database and thumbnail generation are not. Four gigabytes is a reasonable floor for a library of a few hundred titles; eight gigabytes is comfortable; more than sixteen only pays off if you also run virtual machines or containers. On the Synology DS224+, the 2 GB stock configuration is genuinely tight — upgrading to 6 GB is the first thing to do.
 Should I buy a 2-bay or a 4-bay NAS for Plex?
 Buy four bays unless space or budget is genuinely tight. A 2-bay array in RAID 1 wastes half your raw capacity on mirroring, so storing 20 TB requires two 20 TB drives — often more expensive than four 8 TB drives in RAID 5, which would give you 24 TB usable. Four bays also let you expand one drive at a time instead of replacing the whole unit.

 This isn’t a generic “best NAS” list. Those exist, and PCMag writes them better than I can. This is for homelab people: you want a box that stores files and runs Docker containers, hosts a VM or two, feeds Plex/Jellyfin transcoding, and talks fast to your Proxmox cluster over NFS or iSCSI. That narrows the field to NAS units with real CPUs, enough RAM headroom, and 2.5GbE or better networking.

ARM-only units are out (most VM images and a chunk of container images won’t run), and so are boxes with soldered, non-upgradable RAM under 8GB.
 What’s left is a short list. I evaluated each on four things: CPU performance per dollar, RAM ceiling, out-of-box networking speed, and whether the OS lets you run Docker and VMs without hacks.  And whichever you buy, put it on a UPS. A CyberPower CP1500PFCLCD is the $240 insurance that keeps a hard power cut from corrupting your array. If the NAS sits in a rack, the best rack mount UPS guide covers 1U and 2U units. More on that and the rest of the homelab stack in my Black Friday deals tracker and the Docker containers guide .
 FAQ
 What is the best NAS for a homelab in 2026? For most homelabs, the UGREEN DXP4800 Plus: $656.99 on Oct 23, 10GbE plus 2.5GbE, 4 bays plus 2 NVMe slots, RAM up to 64GB, and official support for running TrueNAS, Unraid or Proxmox instead of UGOS. Under $400, the DXP2800. If you want the best software and don’t need hardware transcoding, the Synology DS925+.
 Which hard drives should I put in a NAS? CMR NAS drives: Seagate IronWolf or IronWolf Pro, WD Red Plus or Red Pro, Toshiba N300. Avoid SMR drives in any RAID or ZFS pool. On Oct 23 the best new-drive value I found was the Seagate IronWolf 12TB at $449.99 ($37.50 per TB) from a third-party seller. A renewed Exos X24 was cheaper per TB, with a refurbisher warranty instead of Seagate’s.
 Can these NAS units run Docker containers directly? Yes. All three support Docker natively (UGREEN and Synology have container managers in their OS; TerraMaster supports Docker in TOS). For heavier VM workloads, the UGREEN and TerraMaster hardware handles it; the Synology’s 4GB of base RAM needs an upgrade first.
 Do I need 10GbE for a homelab NAS? Not strictly. 2.5GbE saturates HDDs fine (~280MB/s). 10GbE matters when you add NVMe pools, run VM disks over NFS/iSCSI, or have multiple clients hitting the NAS at once. The DXP4800 Plus having it at $657 removes the dilemma.
 What's the Synology drive whitelist issue? The DS925+ generation only supports drives on Synology’s compatibility list, which favors Synology-branded and enterprise drives and excludes many popular WD/Seagate models. It’s the main reason long-time Synology users have been defecting to UGREEN and DIY builds.
 NAS or just a big USB drive on my mini PC? A DAS enclosure on a mini PC is cheaper and simpler for single-server setups. Buy the NAS when you want RAID management, snapshots, and backups handled by software designed for it, or when storage needs to stay up while your compute boxes get experimented on.
 How much RAM do I need for Docker on a NAS? 8GB runs a handful of containers. If you’re adding Immich, a Plex instance, a couple of databases, and maybe a Home Assistant VM, 32GB is where it stops being tight. That’s why the F4-424 Pro shipping with 32GB matters.

 Best 4-Bay NAS 2026: Picks by Budget and Use Case
 Updated: 2026-07-19 · Last verified July 2026 
 10 min read
 TL;DR A 4-bay NAS is the sweet spot because it's the first size where parity RAID pays off: RAID 5 keeps three drives of usable space with single-drive protection, and RAID 6 adds a second parity drive once you fit large disks. For a no-lock-in default we'd take the Ugreen DH4300 Plus on a budget or the Intel DXP4800 Plus for performance; the Synology DS925+ is the pick if you value polished software, and the QNAP TS-464 is the feature-rich middle with Quick Sync for Plex. The one thing to remember: at 12 TB drives and up, run RAID 6, and back up regardless: parity is not a backup.
 The four-bay NAS is the most-searched device class for a reason: it's the point where a network drive stops being a glorified USB enclosure and becomes a real storage server. Four bays give you enough drives to run efficient parity RAID, enough capacity to grow for years, and enough CPU and RAM options to add Plex, Docker, or a personal cloud later, all without the price and power draw of a six- or eight-bay tower. The trick is matching the right model to what you'll actually do with it, because a budget ARM box and an Intel performance unit are separated by a factor of two in price and a world of difference in what they can run.
 RAID 5 or RAID 6 across four drives? Fill all four bays with 8 TB and watch usable capacity and protection change between single and double parity. 
 Open calculator → 
 Why four bays is the sweet spot
 The reason four bays sit at the centre of the market is efficiency of protection. A two-drive mirror spends half your capacity on redundancy, but the moment you have four drives you can run RAID 5 (single parity spread across all disks) and lose only one drive's worth of space, so four 8 TB drives give you roughly 24 TB usable instead of the 16 TB a mirror would leave. That jump from 50% to 75% capacity efficiency is exactly why people who outgrow a 2-bay tend to skip straight past three bays and land on four, and you can see the trade-off yourself with the which RAID level should you choose guide.
 Four bays also give you a real growth path without over-buying. You can start with two or three drives and add more later, or begin with modest 8 TB disks and swap up to larger ones over time as prices fall, which our 2-bay to 4-bay to 6-bay upgrade guide walks through in detail. A six- or eight-bay chassis costs more, draws more power, and makes more noise for capacity you won't use for years, so for the overwhelming majority of home and prosumer buyers the honest recommendation is simple: a 4-bay is the box that fits your needs today and still has room for the ones you'll have in three years.
 What to look for: CPU, RAM, ports and ecosystem
 The spec sheet on a 4-bay NAS decides far more than raw storage, because these boxes double as small servers. The single most important choice is the processor class, and it splits cleanly into two camps. An ARM chip is fine for file storage, backups, and light app duty, and it sips power while doing it; an Intel processor, usually an N-series part in this class, costs more but unlocks Docker containers, virtual machines, snapshot-capable filesystems, and, crucially for media servers, hardware video transcoding. If you want the NAS to be an app platform rather than a file drawer, that Intel line is where the money goes.
 Beyond the CPU, four things separate a good buy from a frustrating one, and they're worth checking on the spec sheet before you order:
 RAM and whether it's upgradable : 8 GB is a comfortable floor for apps; a SODIMM slot you can fill yourself later is worth more than a soldered chip you can't.
 Networking : 2.5GbE is now the sensible baseline and clears the old gigabit ceiling, while 10GbE or a spare PCIe slot future-proofs a performance build, as we cover in the 2.5GbE NAS upgrade guide.
 NVMe cache or storage slots : one or two M.2 slots let you add read/write cache or an all-flash volume, though some vendors lock these to their own SSDs.
 Ecosystem and OS : the software you'll live in daily, from Synology's polished DSM to QNAP's feature-dense QTS to Ugreen's newer UGOS, plus DIY options if you'd rather run TrueNAS.
 Match those four against your plans and the shortlist writes itself: a light user wants an efficient ARM box with 2.5GbE, while a Plex-and-Docker household wants Intel, 8 GB of upgradable RAM, and NVMe headroom. Our 2026 NAS buying guide compares the platforms in more depth if you're still deciding between vendors.
 The ecosystem question: Synology, QNAP, Ugreen or DIY
 Which brand you buy shapes your experience as much as the hardware, and in 2026 the three main names each pull in a different direction. Synology still ships the most polished software (DSM is the reference for beginner-friendly setup, mobile apps, and backup tooling), but the company has drifted toward locking its newer Plus models to branded drives and branded NVMe SSDs, so the trade for that polish is less freedom over what you put inside; the Synology company background on Wikipedia gives the fuller history. QNAP sits in the feature-rich middle: its QTS software offers more knobs, more apps, and often more ports per dollar than Synology, at the cost of a busier interface that can overwhelm a first-time buyer, and you can read the QNAP company profile on Wikipedia for context.
 Ugreen is the value insurgent, and it's the route we most often point new buyers toward when hardware-per-dollar matters. Its NASync line accepts any standard NAS drive with no compatibility lock, lets you add your own RAM and NVMe, and undercuts the incumbents on networking, so you get more machine for the money; the newer UGOS software is less mature than DSM but improving quickly, as we detail in the Synology vs Ugreen comparison . If you'd rather own the whole stack, a DIY build on a low-power Intel board running TrueNAS or OpenMediaVault gives you total control, which the Synology vs QNAP vs DIY breakdown weighs against the turnkey options. The honest summary: buy Synology for software calm, QNAP for features, Ugreen for value, and DIY for control.
 RAID 5 or RAID 6 on a 4-bay
 Once you've picked the box, the configuration question that matters most is single versus double parity, and the answer hinges on drive size. On a 4-bay filled with drives up to about 8 TB, RAID 5 is a reasonable default: you get three drives of usable space, the array survives one drive failing, and rebuilds finish quickly enough that the risk window stays small. That efficiency is the whole appeal of four bays over a mirror, and for a modest home NAS it's a perfectly sound choice.
 The calculus changes as drives get bigger. When you fit 12 TB or larger disks, a rebuild after a failure can take a day or more, and during that stretch every remaining drive is read end to end, which raises the odds that a second drive fails or hits an unrecoverable read error before the rebuild completes, taking the whole array with it. That's why RAID 6 , with two parity drives and two of usable space, becomes the safer default at large capacities despite costing one more drive. The concrete takeaway: run RAID 5 on a 4-bay only while the drives stay at or below roughly 8 TB, and switch to RAID 6 the moment you're filling it with 12 TB drives or larger.
 The outlier in this class is Ubiquiti's UniFi UNAS 4 at $379, a four-bay desktop box powered over PoE, with the rackmount UNAS Pro 4 above it at $499 adding dual 10-gigabit SFP+ ports and two NVMe cache slots. Both run UniFi Drive , which covers SMB shares, snapshots, per-share encryption, Time Machine and cloud backup and then deliberately stops: no Docker, no virtual machines, no Plex and no hardware transcoding. That rules it out for most of the reasons people buy an Intel four-bay in the first place, and makes it an unusually strong buy in the one case it fits, which is a pure file and backup target on a network you already run with UniFi gear.

 Whatever chassis you pick, pair it with matched CMR NAS drives rather than a mix of sizes, because parity RAID sizes every disk down to the smallest one and any difference is wasted. For a 4-bay, 8 TB is the value sweet spot (see our best 8 TB NAS drive guide), and you can start with three drives and add the fourth later. If you'd prefer a complete shopping list with device, drives, and a UPS bundled per budget tier, the NAS starter kits guide lays out full setups at three price points.
 For the more technical crowd: why Intel Quick Sync matters for Plex
 Here's the one advanced note worth flagging rather than burying: if you plan to run Plex or Jellyfin and expect the server to transcode video on the fly (reformatting a 4K file down to 1080p for a phone or a bandwidth-limited connection), the CPU's built-in video engine does the heavy lifting, not the general-purpose cores. Intel's N-series chips include Quick Sync Video , a fixed-function hardware encoder that transcodes several 4K streams at once while barely touching CPU load, which is exactly why the Intel-based 4-bays, the QNAP TS-464 and Ugreen DXP4800 Plus, run circles around ARM boxes for media serving. The flip side is worth stating plainly for calibration: this class of NAS almost universally lacks ECC memory , the error-correcting RAM that server-grade builds use to catch bit flips, so if silent data integrity at scale is your priority, that's a reason to look at a DIY ZFS build instead. For everyone else, direct-play plus occasional Quick Sync transcoding is the practical target, and any Intel 4-bay here handles it comfortably.
 Plan your usable capacity Four 8 TB drives: 24 TB usable in RAID 5, 16 TB in RAID 6. See the parity trade-off live. 
 Open calculator → 
 Recommendation
 For a first serious NAS that stores files, backs up your machines, and streams a modest media library, the Ugreen DH4300 Plus is the no-lock-in budget default: 8 GB of RAM, 2.5GbE, and any-drive compatibility at an ARM price. If you want a media server that transcodes 4K on demand and don't mind a busier interface, the QNAP TS-464 is the feature-rich middle with Quick Sync and dual 2.5GbE. Prefer the calmest, most beginner-friendly software? Take the Synology DS925+ for its Ryzen headroom, or the cheaper DS425+ if budget is tight; just verify the drive compatibility list first. And if you want maximum performance with 10GbE, upgradable DDR5, and a PCIe slot to grow into, the Ugreen DXP4800 Plus is the prosumer pick. Whichever you choose, run RAID 6 once you fit 12 TB drives, and keep a separate backup, because parity protects against a dead drive but never against a bad delete.
 Frequently asked questions
 Why is a 4-bay NAS considered the sweet spot? Four bays are the first point where parity RAID makes sense: RAID 5 protects four drives while losing only one drive's worth of space, so you keep about three quarters of your raw capacity instead of half. That is far more efficient than a 2-bay mirror, and a 4-bay costs and consumes much less than a 6- or 8-bay tower you would only half-fill for years. It gives room to grow while staying affordable, which is why it is the most searched device class.
 Should I run RAID 5 or RAID 6 on a 4-bay NAS? On a 4-bay with drives up to roughly 8 TB, RAID 5 is a reasonable default and gives you three drives of usable space with single-drive protection. Once you fit 12 TB or larger drives, the multi-day rebuild after a failure raises the odds of a second drive dying during the rebuild, so RAID 6 (double parity, two drives of usable space) becomes the safer choice at the cost of one drive. Compare both live in the RAID calculator before you commit.
 Does the CPU matter on a 4-bay NAS? For plain file storage and backups, an ARM chip with 4-8 GB of RAM is enough. An Intel N-series CPU matters when you run Plex or Jellyfin with on-the-fly transcoding, because its Quick Sync hardware video engine handles multiple 4K streams that an ARM chip cannot. Intel also unlocks Docker containers, virtual machines and snapshot-capable filesystems, so pick Intel if you want the NAS to be an app server rather than just a file store.
 Which 4-bay NAS avoids drive and hardware lock-in? Ugreen's DH4300 Plus and DXP4800 Plus accept any standard NAS drive and let you add your own RAM and NVMe, which is the most open route in this class. Synology delivers the most polished software but has moved toward branded-drive and branded-SSD requirements on newer models, so check the compatibility list first. QNAP sits in the middle with a feature-rich OS and open drive support.
